title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: The ball was only just beginning as Kitty and her mother walked up the great staircase, which was flooded with light and lined with flowers and footmen in powder and red coats. From the rooms came a steady, constant hum, like a hive, and the rustle of movement; and while on the landing, between the trees, they gave their hair and dresses one last check in the mirror, they heard from the ballroom the careful, distinct notes of the orchestra's violins beginning the first waltz. A little old man in civilian clothes, arranging his gray curls before another mirror and giving off a strong scent, bumped into them on the stairs and stood aside, evidently admiring Kitty, whom he did not know. A beardless youth — one of those society youths the old Prince Shtcherbatsky called "young bucks" — in a strikingly low-cut waistcoat, straightening his white tie as he walked, bowed to them, and after running past, came back to ask Kitty for a quadrille. As the first quadrille had already been given to Vronsky, she had to promise this youth the second. An officer, buttoning his glove, stood aside in the doorway, and, stroking his mustache, admired rosy Kitty.

Although her dress, her hair, and all the preparations for the ball had cost Kitty enormous trouble and consideration, at this moment she walked into the ballroom in her elaborate tulle gown over a pink slip as easily and naturally as if all the rosettes and lace, all the tiny details of her outfit, had not cost her or her family a moment's attention — as if she had been born in that tulle and lace, with her hair piled high on her head and a rose with two leaves on top of it.

When, just before going into the ballroom, the princess, her mother, tried to set the ribbon of her sash the right way round, Kitty had drawn back slightly. She felt that everything must be right of itself, and graceful, and that nothing should need adjusting.

It was one of Kitty's best days. Her dress was not uncomfortable anywhere; her lace berthe did not droop anywhere; her rosettes were not crushed or torn off; her pink slippers with their high, hollowed-out heels did not pinch but gladdened her feet; and the thick coil of fair chignon stayed put on her head as though it were her own hair. Every one of the three buttons on the long glove that covered her hand without hiding its lines fastened without tearing. The black velvet of her locket nestled with special softness around her neck. That velvet was delicious; at home, looking at her neck in the mirror, Kitty had felt that velvet was speaking. About everything else there could be doubts, but the velvet was delicious. Kitty smiled here too, at the ball, when she caught sight of it in the glass. Her bare shoulders and arms gave her a feeling of cool marble, a sensation she particularly liked. Her eyes sparkled, and her rosy lips could not help smiling from the awareness of her own attractiveness. She had hardly entered the ballroom and reached the throng of ladies — all tulle, ribbons, lace, and flowers — waiting to be asked to dance (Kitty was never one of that throng) when she was asked for a waltz, and by the best partner of all: the first star in the hierarchy of the ballroom, a renowned director of dances, a married man, handsome and well-built, Yegorushka Korsunsky. He had only just left Countess Bonina, with whom he had danced the first half of the waltz, and, surveying his kingdom — that is, the few couples who had started dancing — he caught sight of Kitty coming in and flew up to her with that special easy amble peculiar to ball directors. Without even asking whether she cared to dance, he held out his arm to encircle her slender waist. She looked round for someone to take her fan, and their hostess, smiling at her, took it.

"How nice that you've come in good time," he said, embracing her waist; "such a bad habit, being late." Bending her left hand, she laid it on his shoulder, and her little feet in their pink slippers began moving over the slippery floor swiftly, lightly, and rhythmically in time to the music.

"It's a rest to waltz with you," he said to her as they fell into the first slow steps of the waltz. "It's exquisite — such lightness, such precision." He said the same thing to almost all the partners he knew well.

She smiled at his praise and went on looking over his shoulder around the room. She was not like a girl at her first ball, for whom every face in the ballroom melts into a single fairyland vision. And she was not a girl who had gone through the stale round of balls until every face was familiar and tiresome. She was somewhere between the two; she was excited, yet had enough self-possession to be able to observe. In the left corner of the ballroom she saw the cream of society gathered. There — incredibly bare-shouldered — was the beauty Lidi, Korsunsky's wife; there was the lady of the house; there shone the bald head of Krivin, always to be found wherever the best people gathered. In that direction the young men gazed, not venturing to approach. There, too, she spotted Stiva, and there she saw the exquisite figure and head of Anna in a black velvet gown. And _he_ was there. Kitty had not seen him since the evening she refused Levin. With her long-sighted eyes she recognized him at once, and was even aware that he was looking at her.
"Another turn? You're not tired?" said Korsunsky, slightly out of breath.
"No, thank you!"
"Where shall I take you?"
"Madame Karenina is here, I think... take me to her."
"Wherever you command."

And Korsunsky began waltzing with measured steps straight toward the group in the left corner, all the while saying "Pardon, mesdames, pardon, pardon, mesdames"; and, steering his course through the sea of lace, tulle, and ribbon without disarranging a single feather, he turned his partner sharply round, so that her slim ankles in light transparent stockings were exposed to view, and her train floated out fan-shaped and covered Krivin's knees. Korsunsky bowed, set his open shirt-front straight, and offered her his arm to lead her to Anna Arkadyevna. Kitty, flushed, took her train off Krivin's knees and, slightly giddy, looked round for Anna. Anna was not in lilac, as Kitty had so urgently wished, but in a black, low-cut velvet gown that revealed her full throat and shoulders, which looked as if carved in old ivory, and her rounded arms with their tiny, slender wrists. The whole gown was trimmed with Venetian guipure. On her head, among her black hair — her own, with no false additions — was a little wreath of pansies, and a bouquet of the same in the black ribbon of her sash among white lace. Her coiffure was not striking. All that was noticeable were the little willful tendrils of her curly hair that kept escaping around her neck and temples. Round her well-cut, strong neck was a single thread of pearls.

Kitty had been seeing Anna every day; she adored her, and had always pictured her in lilac. But now, seeing her in black, she felt that she hadn't really seen her charm at all. She saw her now as someone quite new and surprising. Now she understood that Anna could not have been in lilac, and that her charm was precisely that she always stood out from her clothes, that her dress could never be the noticeable thing on her. And her black dress, with its sumptuous lace, was not noticeable on her either; it was only the frame, and all you saw was her — simple, natural, elegant, and at the same time gay and eager.
Standing as upright as ever, she had her head turned slightly toward the master of the house and was saying something to him just as Kitty came up to the group.

"No, I don't throw stones," she was saying in answer to something, "though I can't understand it," she went on, shrugging, and she turned at once with a soft, protective smile toward Kitty. With a quick, feminine glance she took in her outfit and made a tiny movement of her head — barely visible, but understood by Kitty — signaling approval of her dress and her looks. "You came into the room dancing," she added.

"This is one of my most loyal supporters," Korsunsky said, bowing to Anna Arkadyevna, whom he hadn't yet seen. "The princess does her part to make balls happy and successful. Anna Arkadyevna — a waltz?" he said, bending toward her.
"Have you met?" their host asked.
"Is there anyone we haven't met? My wife and I are like white wolves — everyone knows us," Korsunsky answered. "A waltz, Anna Arkadyevna?"
"I don't dance when it's possible not to dance," she said.
"But tonight it's impossible," Korsunsky replied.
At that instant Vronsky came up.
"Well, since it's impossible tonight, let's start," she said, ignoring Vronsky's bow, and quickly put her hand on Korsunsky's shoulder.

"What is she angry at him about?" Kitty thought, noticing that Anna had deliberately not responded to Vronsky's bow. Vronsky came over to Kitty, reminding her of the first quadrille, and expressing his regret that he hadn't seen her in all this time. Kitty gazed in admiration at Anna waltzing and listened to him. She was expecting him to ask her for a waltz, but he did not, and she glanced at him in surprise. He flushed slightly and hurriedly asked her to waltz, but he had only just put his arm around her waist and taken the first step when the music suddenly stopped. Kitty looked into his face, so close to her own, and long afterwards — for years afterwards — that look, full of love, to which he gave no response, cut her to the heart with shame's agony.
"_Pardon! pardon!_ Waltz! Waltz!" Korsunsky shouted from the other side of the room, and, seizing the first young lady he came across, started dancing himself.

title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: Vronsky and Kitty waltzed several times around the room. After the first waltz Kitty went to her mother, and she had barely had time to say a few words to Countess Nordston when Vronsky came back for the first quadrille. During the quadrille nothing of any significance was said: there was disjointed talk between them about the Korsunskys, husband and wife, whom he described very amusingly as delightful children at forty, and about the future town theater; and only once did the conversation cut her to the quick, when he asked about Levin, whether he was here, and added that he liked him very much. But Kitty was not expecting much from the quadrille. She was looking forward with a thrill at her heart to the mazurka. She imagined that the mazurka would decide everything. The fact that during the quadrille he did not ask her for the mazurka did not worry her. She felt sure she would dance the mazurka with him as she had at past balls, and refused five other young men, saying she was engaged for the mazurka. The whole ball up to the last quadrille was for Kitty an enchanted vision of delightful colors, sounds, and movements. She only sat down when she was too tired and asked for a rest. But as she was dancing the last quadrille with one of the tiresome young men she could not refuse, she happened to be _vis-à-vis_ with Vronsky and Anna. She had not been near Anna again since the beginning of the evening, and now once more she saw her suddenly as quite new and surprising. She saw in her the signs of that thrill of success she knew so well in herself; she saw that Anna was drunk with the wine of admiration she was provoking. She knew that feeling and its signs, and saw them in Anna: the quivering, flashing light in her eyes, the smile of happiness and excitement playing unconsciously on her lips, the deliberate grace, precision, and lightness in her movements.

"Who?" she asked herself. "All of them, or one?" And without helping the harried young man she was dancing with through the conversation, the thread of which he had lost and could not pick up again, she obeyed with outward liveliness Korsunsky's peremptory shouts as he sent them all into the _grand rond_, then into the _chaîne_, and all the while she kept watch, her heart aching more and more. "No, it's not the admiration of the crowd that's intoxicated her, but the adoration of one man. And that one man — could it be him?" Every time he spoke to Anna the joyous light flashed in her eyes, and the smile of happiness curved her red lips. She seemed to be making an effort to hold herself in, to try not to show these signs of pleasure, but they came out on her face of themselves. "But what about him?" Kitty looked at him and was filled with terror. What was pictured so clearly in the mirror of Anna's face she saw in him. What had become of his always self-possessed, resolute manner, the carelessly serene expression on his face? Now, every time he turned to her, he bent his head as though he would have fallen at her feet, and in his eyes there was nothing but humble submission and dread. "I wouldn't offend you," his eyes seemed to be saying every time, "but I want to save myself, and I don't know how." On his face was a look such as Kitty had never seen before.

They were speaking about mutual acquaintances, keeping up the most trivial conversation, but it seemed to Kitty that every word they said was determining their fate and hers. And strange it was that they were really talking about how absurd Ivan Ivanovitch was with his French, and how the Eletsky girl might have made a better match, and yet these words held real weight for them, and they felt about them just as Kitty did. The whole ball, the whole world, everything seemed lost in fog to Kitty's soul. Nothing but the stern discipline of her upbringing kept her going and forced her to do what was expected — to dance, to answer questions, to talk, even to smile. But just before the mazurka, when the chairs were being rearranged and a few couples moved out of the smaller rooms into the big room, a moment of despair and horror came over Kitty. She had refused five partners and now she had no mazurka. She had no hope of being asked for it now, either, because she was so much in demand in society that no one would have thought she had remained free until now. She would have to tell her mother she felt ill and go home, but she did not have the strength to do it. She felt crushed. She went to the farthest corner of the little drawing-room and sank into a low chair. Her light, transparent skirts billowed up like a cloud around her slender waist; one bare, thin, soft, girlish arm, hanging limp, was lost in the folds of her pink tunic; in the other she held her fan and with rapid, short strokes fanned her burning face. But while she looked like a butterfly clinging to a blade of grass, just about to open its rainbow wings for fresh flight, her heart ached with a terrible despair.
"But perhaps I'm wrong, perhaps it wasn't like that?" And again she went over everything she had seen.
"Kitty, what is it?" said Countess Nordston, stepping noiselessly over the carpet toward her. "I don't understand this."
Kitty's lower lip began to quiver; she got up quickly.
"Kitty, you're not dancing the mazurka?"
"No, no," said Kitty, her voice shaking with tears.

"He asked her for the mazurka in front of me," said Countess Nordston, knowing Kitty would understand who "he" and "her" were. "She said, 'Why, aren't you going to dance it with Princess Shtcherbatskaya?'"
"Oh, I don't care!" Kitty answered.
No one but Kitty herself understood her position; no one else knew that she had just turned down the man she perhaps loved — and turned him down because of her faith in another.
Countess Nordston found Korsunsky, with whom she was to dance the mazurka, and told him to ask Kitty.

Kitty danced in the first couple, and luckily for her she did not have to talk because Korsunsky was running about the whole time directing the figure. Vronsky and Anna were sitting almost opposite her. She saw them with her long-sighted eyes, and saw them up close too when they met in the figures, and the more she saw of them the more convinced she became that her unhappiness was complete. She saw that they felt themselves alone in that crowded room. And on Vronsky's face, always so firm and independent, she saw the look that had struck her — that bewilderment and humble submission, like the expression of an intelligent dog that has done wrong.

Anna smiled, and her smile was reflected on his face. She grew thoughtful, and he became serious. Some supernatural force drew Kitty's eyes to Anna's face. She was fascinating in her simple black dress; her round arms with their bracelets were fascinating; her firm neck with its thread of pearls was fascinating; the stray curls of her loose hair were fascinating; the graceful, light movements of her little feet and hands were fascinating; that lovely face in its eagerness was fascinating; but there was something terrible and cruel in her fascination.

Kitty admired her more than ever, and her suffering grew more and more acute. Kitty felt overwhelmed, and her face showed it. When Vronsky saw her, coming up to her in the mazurka, he did not at first recognize her, she was so changed.
"Delightful ball!" he said to her, for the sake of saying something.
"Yes," she answered.

Halfway through the mazurka, repeating a complicated figure newly invented by Korsunsky, Anna came forward into the middle of the circle, chose two gentlemen, and summoned a lady and Kitty. Kitty gazed at her in dismay as she went up. Anna looked at her with drooping eyelids and smiled, pressing her hand. But noticing that Kitty answered her smile only with a look of despair and amazement, she turned away from her and began chattering gaily with the other lady.
"Yes, there is something uncanny, devilish, and fascinating about her," Kitty said to herself.
Anna did not mean to stay for supper, but the host began pressing her to do so.
"Nonsense, Anna Arkadyevna," said Korsunsky, slipping her bare arm beneath the sleeve of his dress coat, "I've an idea for a _cotillion! Un bijou!_"
And he moved her gradually on, trying to draw her along with him. The host smiled approvingly.
"No, I'm not going to stay," Anna answered, smiling; but despite her smile, both Korsunsky and the host could tell from the resolute tone that she would not stay.
"No — as it is, I've danced more at your ball in Moscow than I have all winter in Petersburg," said Anna, glancing round at Vronsky, who stood near her. "I need to rest a little before my journey."
"Are you certainly going tomorrow, then?" Vronsky asked.
"Yes, I suppose so," Anna answered, as if surprised at the boldness of his question; but the irrepressible, quivering brilliance of her eyes and her smile set him on fire as she said it.
Anna Arkadyevna did not stay for supper, but went home.

title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: "Yes, there is something in me that's hateful, repulsive," Levin thought as he left the Shtcherbatskys' and walked toward his brother's lodgings. "And I don't get on with other people. Pride, they say. No, I have no pride. If I had any pride, I wouldn't have put myself in such a position." And he pictured Vronsky to himself, happy, good-natured, clever, self-possessed, certainly never put in the awful position he had been in that evening. "Yes, she was bound to choose him. That's how it had to be, and I have no one and nothing to blame. I'm the one to blame. What right did I have to imagine she would care to join her life with mine? Who am I and what am I? A nobody, not wanted by anyone or useful to anybody." And he remembered his brother Nikolay, and dwelt with pleasure on the thought of him. "Isn't he right that everything in the world is base and loathsome? And are we fair in our judgment of brother Nikolay? Of course, from Prokofy's point of view, seeing him in a torn cloak and tipsy, he's a despicable person. But I know him differently. I know his soul, and I know that we're like him. And I, instead of going to find him, went out to dinner, and came here." Levin walked up to a lamppost, read his brother's address from his pocketbook, and called a sledge. The whole long way to his brother's, Levin vividly recalled all the facts of his brother Nikolay's life that were familiar to him. He remembered how at the university, and for a year afterward, his brother had, despite the mockery of his companions, lived like a monk, strictly observing all religious rites, services, and fasts, and avoiding every kind of pleasure, especially women. And how afterward he had broken out all at once: had run with the most horrible people, plunged into the most senseless debauchery. He remembered the later scandal over a boy whom he had brought from the country to bring up, and, in a fit of rage, had beaten so violently that proceedings were brought against him for unlawful wounding. Then he remembered the scandal with a sharper to whom he had lost money and given a promissory note, and against whom he had himself lodged a complaint, claiming he had cheated him. (This was the money Sergey Ivanovitch had paid.) Then he remembered the night he had spent in the lockup for disorderly conduct in the street. He remembered the shameful proceedings he had tried to bring against his brother Sergey Ivanovitch, accusing him of not having paid him his share of their mother's fortune, and the latest scandal — when he had gone to a western province in an official capacity and got into trouble for assaulting a village elder... It was all horribly disgusting, and yet to Levin it appeared in nothing like the disgusting light it inevitably would to those who did not know Nikolay, did not know his whole story, did not know his heart.

Levin remembered that when Nikolay had been in his devout phase — the period of fasts and monks and church services, when he had been looking to religion for a support and a curb for his passionate nature — far from encouraging him, everyone, including Levin himself, had jeered at him. They had teased him, called him Noah and the monk; and when he had broken out, no one had helped him, but everyone had turned away from him with horror and disgust.

Levin felt that, in spite of all the ugliness of his life, his brother Nikolay, in his soul, in the very depths of his soul, was no more in the wrong than the people who despised him. He was not to blame for having been born with his unbridled temperament and his somehow limited intelligence. But he had always wanted to be good. "I'll tell him everything, hold nothing back, and I'll make him speak openly to me too, and I'll show him that I love him and so understand him," Levin resolved to himself, as he reached the hotel he had the address of, around eleven o'clock.
"At the top, 12 and 13," the porter answered Levin's inquiry.
"At home?"
"Sure to be at home."

The door of No. 12 was half open, and out into the streak of light came thick fumes of cheap, poor tobacco and the sound of a voice unknown to Levin; but he knew at once that his brother was there — he heard his cough.
As he went in the door, the unknown voice was saying:
"It all depends with how much judgment and knowledge the thing's done."

Konstantin Levin looked in at the door, and saw that the speaker was a young man with an enormous shock of hair wearing a Russian jerkin, and that a pockmarked woman in a woolen gown, without collar or cuffs, was sitting on the sofa. His brother was not in sight. Konstantin felt a sharp pang at his heart at the thought of the strange company in which his brother spent his life. No one had heard him, and Konstantin, taking off his galoshes, listened to what the man in the jerkin was saying. He was talking about some sort of enterprise.
"Well, the devil take them, the privileged classes," his brother's voice responded, with a cough. "Masha! Get us some supper and some wine if any's left; if not, go and get some."
The woman got up, came out from behind the screen, and saw Konstantin.
"There's some gentleman here, Nikolay Dmitrievitch," she said.
"Whom do you want?" said Nikolay Levin's voice, angrily.
"It's me," answered Konstantin Levin, stepping forward into the light.

"Who's _me?_" Nikolay's voice asked again, even angrier. He could be heard getting up hurriedly, stumbling against something, and Levin saw, facing him in the doorway, the big, scared eyes and huge, thin, stooping figure of his brother — so familiar and yet astonishing in its weirdness and sickliness.

He had grown even thinner than three years ago, when Konstantin Levin had last seen him. He was wearing a short coat, and his hands and big bones looked larger than ever. His hair had thinned, the same straight mustaches covered his lips, the same eyes stared strangely and naïvely at his visitor.

"Ah, Kostya!" he exclaimed suddenly, recognizing his brother, and his eyes lit up with joy. But the same second he glanced at the young man and gave that nervous jerk of his head and neck Konstantin knew so well, as though his neckband were hurting him; and a quite different expression — wild, suffering, cruel — settled on his emaciated face.
"I wrote to you and Sergey Ivanovitch both that I don't know you and don't want to know you. What is it you want?"

He was nothing like what Konstantin had been picturing. The worst and most tiresome side of his character — what made all relations with him so difficult — had been forgotten by Konstantin Levin when he thought of him, and now, seeing his face, and especially that nervous twitching of his head, he remembered it all.
"I didn't want to see you for anything," he answered timidly. "I've simply come to see you."
His brother's timidity obviously softened Nikolay. His lips twitched.

"Oh, so that's it?" he said. "Well, come in, sit down. Like some supper? Masha, bring supper for three. No, wait. Do you know who this is?" he said, addressing his brother and pointing to the man in the jerkin. "This is Mr. Kritsky, a friend of mine from Kiev, a very remarkable man. The police are after him, of course, because he's not a scoundrel."

And he looked round the room the way he always did at everyone in it. Seeing that the woman standing in the doorway was about to leave, he shouted at her, "Wait a minute, I said." And with the inability to express himself, the incoherence that Konstantin knew so well, he began, with another look round at everyone, to tell his brother Kritsky's story: how he had been expelled from the university for starting a benefit society for poor students and Sunday schools; how he had then been a teacher in a peasant school, had been driven out of that too, and had afterward been tried for something.
"You're from Kiev university?" Konstantin Levin said to Kritsky, to break the awkward silence that followed.
"Yes, I was at Kiev," Kritsky replied angrily, his face darkening.

"And this woman," Nikolay Levin cut in, pointing to her, "is the partner of my life, Marya Nikolaevna. I took her out of a bad house" — and he jerked his neck as he said it — "but I love her and respect her, and anyone who wants to know me," he added, raising his voice and knitting his brows, "I ask to love her and respect her too. She's just the same as my wife, just the same. So now you know whom you have to deal with. And if you think you're lowering yourself, well, there's the floor, there's the door."
And again his eyes traveled inquiringly over them all.
"Why I should be lowering myself, I don't understand."
"Then, Masha, tell them to bring supper; three portions, spirits and wine... No, wait... No, it doesn't matter... Go on."

title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: "So you see," Nikolay Levin went on, painfully wrinkling his forehead and twitching.
It was clearly hard for him to think of what to say and do.

"Here, do you see?"... He pointed to some kind of iron bars, fastened together with string, lying in a corner of the room. "See that? That's the start of a new thing we're going into. It's a productive association..."

Konstantin barely heard him. He looked into his sickly, consumptive face, and felt sorrier for him by the minute, and could not force himself to follow what his brother was telling him about the association. He saw that this association was merely an anchor to save him from self-contempt. Nikolay Levin went on:

"You know that capital oppresses the laborer. With us, the laborers — the peasants — bear all the burden of work, and are so placed that however much they work they can never escape from their position as beasts of burden. All the profits from their labor, on which they might improve their position, gain leisure, and after that education — all the surplus values — are taken from them by the capitalists. And society is so arranged that the harder they work, the greater the profit of the merchants and landowners, while they stay beasts of burden to the end. That state of things has to be changed," he finished, and looked at his brother questioningly.
"Yes, of course," said Konstantin, looking at the patch of red that had come out on his brother's projecting cheekbones.
"And so we're founding a locksmiths' association where all the production and the profit and the chief instruments of production will be held in common."
"Where is the association to be?" asked Konstantin Levin.
"In the village of Vozdrem, Kazan province."
"But why in a village? In the villages, I think, there's plenty of work already. Why a locksmiths' association in a village?"

"Why? Because the peasants are just as much slaves as they ever were, and that's why you and Sergey Ivanovitch don't like it when people try to get them out of their slavery," said Nikolay Levin, exasperated by the objection.
Konstantin Levin sighed, looking around the cheerless, dirty room. The sigh seemed to exasperate Nikolay still more.
"I know your and Sergey Ivanovitch's aristocratic views. I know that he applies all the power of his intellect to justifying existing evils."
"No, and why are you talking about Sergey Ivanovitch?" said Levin, smiling.

"Sergey Ivanovitch? I'll tell you why!" Nikolay Levin shrieked suddenly at the name. "I'll tell you why... But what's the use of talking? There's only one thing... What did you come to me for? You look down on this, and you're welcome to — go away, in God's name, go away!" he shrieked, getting up from his chair. "Go away, go away!"
"I don't look down on it at all," said Konstantin Levin timidly. "I'm not even arguing."
At that instant Marya Nikolaevna came back. Nikolay Levin glanced angrily at her. She went quickly over to him and whispered something.

"I'm not well; I've become irritable," said Nikolay Levin, calming down and breathing painfully; "and then you start in about Sergey Ivanovitch and his article. It's such rubbish, such lying, such self-deception. What can a man write about justice when he knows nothing of it? Have you read his article?" he asked Kritsky, sitting down again at the table and pushing back half the scattered cigarettes to clear a space.
"I haven't read it," Kritsky answered gloomily, obviously not wanting to enter the conversation.
"Why not?" Nikolay Levin asked, now turning his exasperation on Kritsky.
"Because I didn't see the point in wasting my time on it."

"Oh, but excuse me, how did you know it would be a waste of your time? That article is too deep for many people — that is, it's over their heads. But with me it's another matter; I see through his ideas, and I know where its weakness lies."
Everyone was silent. Kritsky got up deliberately and reached for his cap.
"Won't you have supper? All right, good-bye! Come round tomorrow with the locksmith."
Kritsky had barely gone when Nikolay Levin smiled and winked.
"He's no good either," he said. "I can see, of course..."
But at that moment Kritsky, at the door, called him.
"What do you want now?" he said, and went out to him in the passage. Left alone with Marya Nikolaevna, Levin turned to her.
"Have you been with my brother long?" he asked her.
"Yes, more than a year. Nikolay Dmitrievitch's health has got very poor. Nikolay Dmitrievitch drinks a great deal," she said.
"That is... how does he drink?"
"Drinks vodka, and it's bad for him."
"And a great deal?" Levin whispered.
"Yes," she said, looking timidly toward the doorway, where Nikolay Levin had reappeared.
"What were you talking about?" he said, knitting his brows and turning his scared eyes from one to the other. "What was it?"
"Oh, nothing," Konstantin answered in confusion.

"Oh, if you don't want to say, don't. Only it's no use your talking to her. She's a wench, and you're a gentleman," he said with a jerk of the neck. "You understand everything, I see, and have taken stock of everything, and look down with pity on my shortcomings," he began again, raising his voice.
"Nikolay Dmitrievitch, Nikolay Dmitrievitch," whispered Marya Nikolaevna, going up to him again.

"Oh, all right, all right!... But where's the supper? Ah, here it is," he said, seeing a waiter with a tray. "Here, set it here," he added angrily, and, promptly seizing the vodka, he poured out a glassful and drank it greedily. "Like a drink?" he said, turning to his brother, and at once became more good-humored.

"Well, enough of Sergey Ivanovitch. I'm glad to see you, all the same. After all is said and done, we're not strangers. Come, have a drink. Tell me what you're up to," he went on, greedily chewing a piece of bread and pouring out another glassful. "How are you living?"

"I live alone in the country, as I always have. I keep busy looking after the land," Konstantin answered, watching with horror the greediness with which his brother ate and drank, and trying to hide that he noticed.
"Why don't you get married?"
"It hasn't happened," Konstantin answered, reddening a little.

"Why not? For me now... it's all over with me! I've made a mess of my life. But this I've said before, and I'll say again — if my share had been given to me when I needed it, my whole life would have been different."
Konstantin hurried to change the subject.
"Did you know your Vanya is with me, as a clerk in the countinghouse at Pokrovskoe?"
Nikolay jerked his neck and fell into thought.

"Yes — tell me what's happening at Pokrovskoe. Is the house still standing, and the birch trees, and our schoolroom? And Philip the gardener, is he still alive? How I remember the arbor and the seat! Now mind, don't change anything in the house — hurry up and get married, and make everything as it used to be again. Then I'll come and see you, if your wife is nice."
"But come and see me now," said Levin. "How nicely we'd arrange it!"
"I'd come and see you if I were sure I wouldn't find Sergey Ivanovitch there."
"You wouldn't find him there. I live quite independently of him."
"Yes, but say what you like, you'll have to choose between him and me," he said, looking timidly into his brother's face.
This timidity touched Konstantin.

"If you want to hear my profession of faith on the subject, I'll tell you that in your quarrel with Sergey Ivanovitch I take neither side. You're both wrong. You're more wrong on the outside, and he is more wrong inside."
"Ah, ah! You see that, you see that!" Nikolay shouted joyfully.
"But personally I value friendly relations with you more, because..."
"Why? Why?"

Konstantin could not bring himself to say that he valued it more because Nikolay was unhappy and in need of affection. But Nikolay knew that was precisely what he meant to say, and, scowling, picked up the vodka again.
"Enough, Nikolay Dmitrievitch!" Marya Nikolaevna said, stretching out her plump bare arm toward the decanter.
"Let it alone! Don't push me! I'll beat you!" he shouted.
Marya Nikolaevna smiled a sweet, good-humored smile that was at once reflected on Nikolay's face, and she took the bottle.
"And do you imagine she doesn't understand anything?" said Nikolay. "She gets it all, better than any of us. Isn't it true there's something good and sweet in her?"
"Have you ever been in Moscow before?" Konstantin said to her, for the sake of saying something.

"Only you mustn't be polite and stiff with her. It frightens her. No one ever spoke to her like that except the justices of the peace who tried her for trying to get out of a brothel. Mercy on us, the senselessness in the world!" he cried suddenly. "These new institutions, these justices of the peace, rural councils, what hideousness it all is!"
And he began to expand on his encounters with the new institutions.

Konstantin Levin heard him out, and the disbelief in the value of all public institutions — which he himself shared with him and often voiced — was distasteful to him now coming out of his brother's mouth.
"In another world we shall understand it all," he said lightly.

"In another world! Ah, I don't like that other world! I don't like it," he said, letting his scared eyes rest on his brother's. "You'd think that to get out of all the baseness and the mess, one's own and other people's, would be a good thing, and yet I'm afraid of death, terribly afraid of death." He shuddered. "But do drink something. Would you like some champagne? Or shall we go somewhere? Let's go to the Gypsies! Do you know, I've grown so fond of the Gypsies and Russian songs."
His speech had begun to slur, and he jumped from one subject to another. With Masha's help Konstantin persuaded him not to go out anywhere, and got him to bed hopelessly drunk.
Masha promised to write to Konstantin if there was need, and to try to persuade Nikolay Levin to come and stay with his brother.

title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: In the morning Konstantin Levin left Moscow, and toward evening he reached home. On the train journey he talked to his neighbors about politics and the new railways, and just as in Moscow he was overcome by a confusion of ideas, dissatisfaction with himself, shame about something or other. But when he got out at his own station, when he saw his one-eyed coachman Ignat with the collar of his coat turned up; when, in the dim light reflected by the station fires, he saw his own sledge, his own horses with their tails tied up, in their harness trimmed with rings and tassels; when the coachman Ignat, as he was loading the luggage, told him the village news — that the contractor had arrived, and that Pava had calved — he felt the confusion gradually clearing up, and the shame and self-dissatisfaction passing away. He felt this at the mere sight of Ignat and the horses; but when he had put on the sheepskin coat brought for him, had settled himself wrapped up in the sledge and driven off, pondering the work ahead of him in the village and watching the side-horse that had once been his saddle-horse, past its prime now but still a spirited beast from the Don, he began to see what had happened to him in a quite different light. He felt himself, and did not want to be anyone else. All he wanted now was to be better than he had been. In the first place he resolved that from that day on he would give up hoping for the kind of extraordinary happiness marriage was supposed to bring him, and consequently would no longer disdain what he really had. Secondly, he would never again let himself give way to low passion, the memory of which had so tortured him while he was making up his mind to propose. Then, remembering his brother Nikolay, he resolved that he would never allow himself to forget him, that he would keep an eye on him and not lose track of him, so as to be ready to help when things took a bad turn. And that would be soon, he felt. Then, too, his brother's talk of communism, which he had treated so lightly at the time, now made him think. He considered a revolution in economic conditions nonsense. But he had always felt the injustice of his own abundance compared with the poverty of the peasants, and now he resolved that, to feel quite in the right — though he had worked hard and lived no luxurious life before — he would now work still harder and allow himself even less luxury. And all this seemed to him so easy a conquest over himself that he spent the whole drive in the pleasantest daydreams. With a firm sense of hope in a new and better life, he reached home a little before nine at night.

The snow of the little quadrangle in front of the house was lit up by the light in the bedroom windows of his old nurse, Agafea Mihalovna, who performed the duties of housekeeper in his house. She was not asleep yet. Kouzma, woken by her, came shuffling sleepily out onto the steps. A setter, Laska, ran out too, almost knocking Kouzma over, and, whining, circled around Levin's knees, jumping up and longing — but not daring — to put her forepaws on his chest.
"You're back soon, sir," said Agafea Mihalovna.
"I got tired of all of it, Agafea Mihalovna. With friends one is fine; at home one is better," he answered, and went into his study.

The study lit up slowly as the candle was brought in. The familiar details came out: the stag's horns, the bookshelves, the mirror, the stove with its ventilator that had long needed mending, his father's sofa, a large table, on the table an open book, a broken ashtray, a notebook in his own hand. As he saw all this, there came over him for an instant a doubt about being able to arrange the new life he had been dreaming of on the road. All these traces of his life seemed to grab at him and tell him: "No, you're not going to get away from us; you're not going to be any different; you'll go on being the same as you always have — with your doubts, your everlasting dissatisfaction with yourself, your useless attempts to amend, and your falls, and your eternal expectation of a happiness you won't get and which isn't possible for you."

These were the things telling him this, but another voice in his heart was saying that he must not fall under the sway of the past, and that one can do anything with oneself. And on hearing that voice, he went into the corner where his two heavy dumbbells stood and began swinging them like a gymnast, trying to restore his confident mood. There was a creak of steps at the door. He hastily put down the dumbbells.

The bailiff came in and said everything, thank God, was going well; but informed him that the buckwheat in the new drying machine had been a bit scorched. This piece of news irritated Levin. The new drying machine had been built and partly invented by Levin. The bailiff had always been against the drying machine, and now it was with suppressed triumph that he reported the buckwheat had been scorched. Levin was firmly convinced that if the buckwheat had been scorched it was only because the precautions had not been taken that he had given orders about hundreds of times. He was annoyed and gave the bailiff a reprimand. But there had been an important and joyful event: Pava, his best cow, an expensive beast bought at a show, had calved.
"Kouzma, get me my sheepskin. And you, tell them to bring a lantern. I'll come and have a look at her," he said to the bailiff.

The cowhouse for the more valuable cows was just behind the house. Walking across the yard, passing a snowdrift by the lilac tree, he went into the cowhouse. There was the warm, steamy smell of dung as the frozen door opened, and the cows, startled by the unfamiliar light of the lantern, stirred on the fresh straw. He caught a glimpse of the broad, smooth, black-and-piebald back of Hollandka. Berkoot, the bull, was lying down with his ring in his lip, and seemed about to get up, but thought better of it and only gave two snorts as they passed him. Pava, a perfect beauty, huge as a hippopotamus, with her back turned to them, kept them from seeing the calf as she sniffed it all over.

Levin went into the pen, looked Pava over, and lifted the red-and-spotted calf onto her long, tottering legs. Pava, uneasy, started lowing, but when Levin set the calf close to her she calmed down, and, with a heavy sigh, began licking it with her rough tongue. The calf, fumbling, poked her nose under her mother's udder and stiffened her tail out straight.

"Here, Fyodor, bring the light over this way," Levin said, looking the calf over. "She's like the mother — though the color is more like the father; but that's nothing. Very good. Long and broad in the haunch. Vassily Fedorovitch, isn't she splendid?" he said to the bailiff, completely forgiving him about the buckwheat under the spell of his delight in the calf.

"How could she fail to be, sir? Oh, Semyon the contractor came the day after you left. You'll need to settle up with him, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the bailiff said. "I did tell you about the machine."

This one question was enough to plunge Levin back into all the details of his work on the estate, which was on a large and complicated scale. He walked straight from the cowhouse to the counting house, and after a brief talk with the bailiff and Semyon the contractor, returned to the house and went straight upstairs to the drawing-room.

title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: The house was big and old-fashioned, and Levin, though he lived alone, kept the whole house heated and used. He knew it was foolish, knew it was positively wrong and contrary to his new plans, but this house was a whole world to Levin. It was the world in which his father and mother had lived and died. They had lived exactly the life that seemed to Levin the ideal of perfection, and the life he had dreamed of beginning again with his wife, his family.

Levin barely had a memory of his mother. His conception of her was for him a sacred thing, and his future wife was bound to be in his imagination a repetition of that exquisite, holy ideal his mother had been.

He was so far from conceiving of love for a woman apart from marriage that he positively pictured to himself first the family, and only secondly the woman who would give him a family. His ideas about marriage were therefore quite unlike those of the great majority of his acquaintances, for whom getting married was one of the many ordinary facts of social life. For Levin it was the chief business of life, on which all its happiness turned. And now he had to give that up.

When he had gone into the little drawing-room where he always had tea, and had settled himself in his armchair with a book, and Agafea Mihalovna had brought him tea and with her usual "Well, I'll stay a while, sir" had taken a chair by the window, he felt that — strange as it might be — he had not parted from his daydreams, and could not live without them. Whether with her, or with another, still it would be. He was reading a book and thinking about what he was reading, and pausing to listen to Agafea Mihalovna, who gossiped on without flagging; and yet through it all, all kinds of pictures of family life and future work rose disconnectedly before his imagination. He felt that in the depths of his soul something had been put in its place, settled, and laid to rest.

He heard Agafea Mihalovna talking about how Prohor had forgotten his duty to God, and how, with the money Levin had given him to buy a horse, he had been drinking without stopping, and had beaten his wife till he'd half killed her. He listened, and read his book, and went back over the whole train of ideas his reading had set off. It was Tyndall's _Treatise on Heat_. He recalled his own criticisms of Tyndall — of his complacent satisfaction in the cleverness of his experiments, and his lack of philosophic insight. And suddenly a joyful thought floated into his mind: "In two years' time I'll have two Dutch cows; Pava herself will perhaps still be alive, a dozen young daughters of Berkoot and the three others — how lovely!"

He picked up his book again. "Very well, electricity and heat are the same thing; but is it possible to substitute the one quantity for the other in the equation for the solution of any problem? No. Well, then what of it? The connection between all the forces of nature is felt instinctively... It would be particularly nice if Pava's daughter turns out a red-spotted cow, and the whole herd takes after her, and the other three too! Splendid! To go out with my wife and our visitors to meet the herd... My wife says, 'Kostya and I looked after that calf like a child.' 'How can it interest you so much?' says a visitor. 'Everything that interests him interests me.' But who will she be?" And he remembered what had happened in Moscow... "Well, there's nothing to be done... It's not my fault. But now everything shall go on in a new way. It's nonsense to pretend life won't let me, that the past won't let me. One has to struggle to live better, much better."... He raised his head and fell to dreaming. Old Laska, who had not yet fully digested her delight at his return and had run out into the yard to bark, came back wagging her tail, crept up to him bringing with her the scent of fresh air, put her head under his hand, and whined plaintively, asking to be stroked.
"There, who'd have thought it?" said Agafea Mihalovna. "The dog now... she understands that her master has come home and that he's low-spirited."
"Why low-spirited?"
"Do you suppose I can't see it, sir? It's about time I knew the gentry. Why, I've grown up from a tiny thing with them. It's nothing, sir, so long as one has health and a clear conscience."
Levin looked at her intently, surprised at how well she knew his thoughts.
"Shall I fetch you another cup?" she said, and taking his cup she went out.

Laska kept poking her head under his hand. He stroked her, and she promptly curled up at his feet, laying her head on a hind paw. And as a sign that all was now well and satisfactory, she opened her mouth a little, smacked her lips, and, settling her sticky lips more comfortably about her old teeth, she sank into blissful repose. Levin watched all her movements attentively.
"That's what I'll do," he said to himself; "that's what I'll do. Nothing's wrong... All's well."

title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: The morning after the ball, early, Anna Arkadyevna sent her husband a telegram that she was leaving Moscow the same day.

"No, I have to go, I have to go," she explained to her sister-in-law about the change in her plans, in a tone that suggested she had so many things to remember there was no enumerating them: "no, it had really better be today!"
Stepan Arkadyevitch was not dining at home, but he promised to come and see his sister off at seven o'clock.

Kitty did not come either, sending a note that she had a headache. Dolly and Anna dined alone with the children and the English governess. Whether it was that the children were fickle, or that they had keen senses and felt that Anna was quite different that day from what she had been when they had taken such a fancy to her, that she was no longer interested in them — but they had abruptly dropped their play with their aunt, and their love for her, and were quite indifferent that she was leaving. Anna spent the whole morning absorbed in preparations for her departure. She wrote notes to her Moscow acquaintances, did her accounts, and packed. To Dolly it seemed Anna was not in a placid state of mind, but in that worried mood Dolly knew well in herself, the kind that does not come without cause and usually covers dissatisfaction with self. After dinner Anna went up to her room to dress, and Dolly followed her.
"How strange you are today," Dolly said to her.

"I? Do you think so? I'm not strange, but I'm in a nasty mood. I'm like this sometimes. I keep feeling as if I could cry. It's very stupid, but it'll pass," Anna said quickly, and bent her flushed face over a tiny bag in which she was packing a nightcap and some cambric handkerchiefs. Her eyes were unusually bright, and continually filled with tears. "In the same way I didn't want to leave Petersburg, and now I don't want to leave here."
"You came here and did a good deed," said Dolly, looking at her intently.
Anna looked at her with eyes wet with tears.

"Don't say that, Dolly. I've done nothing, and I could do nothing. I often wonder why people are all in league to spoil me. What have I done, and what could I have done? In your heart there was love enough to forgive..."
"If it hadn't been for you, God knows what would have happened! How fortunate you are, Anna," said Dolly. "Everything is clear and good in your heart."
"Every heart has its own _skeletons_, as the English say."
"You don't have any sort of _skeleton_, do you? Everything is so clear in you."
"I do!" said Anna suddenly, and, unexpectedly after her tears, a sly, ironical smile curved her lips.
"Well, then, he's amusing, your _skeleton_, at any rate, and not depressing," said Dolly, smiling.

"No, he's depressing. Do you know why I'm going today instead of tomorrow? It's a confession that's weighing on me, and I want to make it to you," said Anna, letting herself drop firmly into an armchair and looking straight into Dolly's face.
And to her surprise Dolly saw that Anna was blushing up to her ears, up to the curly black ringlets on her neck.

"Yes," Anna went on. "Do you know why Kitty didn't come to dinner? She's jealous of me. I've spoiled... I've been the cause of that ball being a torture to her instead of a pleasure. But truly, truly, it's not my fault, or only my fault a little bit," she said, daintily drawling the words "a little bit."
"Oh, how like Stiva you said that!" Dolly said, laughing.
Anna was hurt.
"Oh, no, oh no! I am not Stiva," she said, frowning. "That's why I'm telling you — because I could never let myself doubt myself for an instant," said Anna.

But at the very moment she was saying the words, she felt they were not true. She was not merely doubting herself; she felt emotion at the thought of Vronsky, and was leaving earlier than she had planned simply to avoid meeting him.
"Yes, Stiva told me you danced the mazurka with him, and that he..."
"You can't imagine how absurdly the whole thing came about. I only meant to do a bit of matchmaking, and instead it turned out quite differently. Possibly against my own will..."
She crimsoned and stopped.
"Oh, they feel it right away?" said Dolly.
"But I'd be in despair if there were anything serious in it on his side," Anna cut in. "And I'm certain it will all be forgotten, and Kitty will stop hating me."

"All the same, Anna, I'll tell you the truth — I'm not very keen on this marriage for Kitty. And it's better for it to come to nothing, if he, Vronsky, is capable of falling in love with you in a single day."

"Oh, heavens, that would be too silly!" said Anna, and once again a deep flush of pleasure spread over her face as she heard the idea that was absorbing her put into words. "And so here I am going off, having made an enemy of Kitty, whom I liked so much! Ah, how sweet she is! But you'll set it right, Dolly? Won't you?"
Dolly could hardly suppress a smile. She loved Anna, but she enjoyed seeing that even she had her weaknesses.
"An enemy? That can't be."
"I did so want all of you to care for me, the way I care for you, and now I care for you more than ever," said Anna, her eyes filling with tears. "Ah, how silly I am today!"
She passed her handkerchief over her face and began dressing.
At the very moment of starting, Stepan Arkadyevitch arrived — late, rosy and good-humored, smelling of wine and cigars.

Anna's emotionalism infected Dolly, and when she embraced her sister-in-law for the last time, she whispered, "Remember, Anna, what you've done for me — I shall never forget. And remember that I love you, and shall always love you as my dearest friend!"
"I don't know why," said Anna, kissing her and hiding her tears.
"You understood me, and you understand. Good-bye, my darling!"

title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: The raging tempest rushed whistling between the wheels of the carriages, around the scaffolding, and round the corner of the station. The carriages, posts, people, everything in sight was covered with snow on one side, and was being thickly covered with more. For a moment there would come a lull in the storm, but then it would swoop down again with such force it seemed impossible to stand against it. Meanwhile men ran back and forth, talking merrily, their steps crackling on the platform as they kept opening and closing the big doors. The bent shadow of a man glided by at her feet, and she heard the sound of a hammer on iron. "Hand over that telegram!" came an angry voice out of the stormy darkness on the other side. "This way! No. 28!" several different voices shouted again, and muffled figures ran by, covered with snow. Two gentlemen with lit cigarettes passed her. She drew another deep breath of the fresh air, and had just taken her hand out of her muff to grab the doorpost and get back into the carriage when another man in a military overcoat, very close beside her, stepped between her and the flickering light of the lamppost. She looked round, and that instant recognized Vronsky's face. Putting his hand to the peak of his cap, he bowed to her and asked whether there was anything she wanted, whether he could be of any service. For a fairly long while she gazed at him without answering, and, in spite of the shadow he was standing in, she saw, or fancied she saw, both the expression of his face and his eyes. It was again that look of reverent ecstasy that had so worked on her the day before. More than once in the past few days, and again only a few moments before, she had told herself that Vronsky was for her only one of the hundreds of young men, forever exactly the same, that one meets everywhere, and that she would never allow herself to give him a thought. But now at the first instant of meeting him, she was seized by a feeling of joyful pride. She had no need to ask why he had come. She knew as certainly as if he had told her that he was here in order to be where she was.
"I didn't realize you were traveling. What have you come for?" she said, letting fall the hand with which she had gripped the doorpost. Irrepressible delight and eagerness lit her face.
"What have I come for?" he repeated, looking straight into her eyes. "You know — I have come to be where you are," he said. "I can't help it."

At that moment the wind, as if overcoming all obstacles, sent the snow flying from the carriage roofs, and clanked some sheet of iron it had torn loose, while the hoarse whistle of the engine roared in front, mournful and gloomy. The whole awfulness of the storm seemed even more splendid to her now. He had said what her soul longed to hear, though she feared it with her reason. She made no answer, and in her face he saw a conflict.
"Forgive me, if you dislike what I said," he said humbly.
He had spoken courteously, deferentially, yet so firmly, so stubbornly, that for a long while she could make no answer.
"What you say is wrong, and I beg you, if you're a good man, to forget what you've said, as I forget it," she said at last.
"Not one word, not one gesture of yours shall I, could I, ever forget..."

"Enough, enough!" she cried, trying hard to give a stern expression to her face, into which he was gazing greedily. And, clutching at the cold doorpost, she clambered up the steps and got rapidly into the corridor of the carriage. But in the little corridor she paused, going over in her mind what had happened. Though she could not recall her own words or his, she sensed instinctively that the moment's conversation had brought them frighteningly closer; and she was panic-stricken and blissful at it. After standing still for a few seconds, she went into the carriage and sat down in her place. The overstrained condition that had tormented her before not only came back but intensified, reaching such a pitch that she was afraid every minute that something would snap inside her from the excessive tension. She did not sleep all night. But in that nervous tension, and in the visions filling her imagination, there was nothing disagreeable or gloomy: on the contrary there was something blissful, glowing, and exhilarating. Toward morning Anna sank into a doze, sitting in her place, and when she woke it was daylight and the train was nearing Petersburg. At once thoughts of home, of husband and son, and the details of that day and the next came over her.

At Petersburg, as soon as the train stopped and she got out, the first person who caught her attention was her husband. "Oh, mercy! why do his ears look like that?" she thought, looking at his frigid and imposing figure, and especially the ears that struck her in that moment as propping up the brim of his round hat. Catching sight of her, he came toward her, his lips falling into their habitual sarcastic smile, his big, tired eyes looking straight at her. An unpleasant sensation gripped at her heart when she met his obstinate and weary glance, as though she had expected to find him different. She was especially struck by the feeling of dissatisfaction with herself that she felt on meeting him. That feeling was an intimate, familiar one, like the consciousness of hypocrisy that she felt in her relations with her husband. But until now she had not noticed the feeling; now she was clearly and painfully aware of it.

"Yes — as you can see, your tender spouse, as devoted as in the first year of our marriage, burned with impatience to see you," he said in his deliberate, high-pitched voice, in the tone he almost always took with her — a tone that mocked anyone who might say in earnest what he was saying.
"Is Seryozha quite well?" she asked.
"And is this all the reward," he said, "for my ardor? He's quite well..."

title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: Vronsky had not even tried to sleep all that night. He sat in his armchair, looking straight before him or scanning the people getting in and out. If he had on previous occasions struck and impressed people who didn't know him with his air of unhesitating composure, he now seemed even more haughty and self-possessed than ever. He looked at people as though they were things. A nervous young man, a clerk in a law court sitting opposite him, hated him for that look. The young man asked him for a light and tried to start a conversation with him, even pushed against him, to make him feel that he was a person, not a thing. But Vronsky looked at him exactly as he did at the lamp, and the young man made a wry face, feeling that he was losing his composure under the oppression of this refusal to recognize him as a person.

Vronsky saw nothing and no one. He felt himself a king — not because he believed he had made an impression on Anna (he did not yet believe that), but because the impression she had made on him filled him with happiness and pride.

What would come of it all he did not know; he did not even think about it. He felt that all his powers, until now scattered and wasted, were now concentrated on one thing, and bent with fearful energy on one blissful goal. And he was happy at it. He knew only that he had told her the truth, that he had come where she was, that all the happiness of his life, the only meaning in life for him, now lay in seeing and hearing her. And when he got out of the carriage at Bologovo for some seltzer water, and caught sight of Anna, his first word had told her, in spite of himself, exactly what he was thinking. And he was glad he had told her, that she knew it now and was thinking about it. He did not sleep all night. Back in the carriage, he kept going over and over every attitude in which he had seen her, every word she had spoken, and before his fancy, making his heart faint with emotion, floated pictures of a possible future.

When he got out of the train at Petersburg, he felt, after his sleepless night, as keen and fresh as if he had just had a cold bath. He paused near his compartment, waiting for her to get out. "Once more," he said to himself, smiling without realizing it, "once more I shall see her walk, her face; she will say something, turn her head, glance, smile, perhaps." But before he caught sight of her, he saw her husband, whom the station-master was deferentially escorting through the crowd. "Ah, yes! The husband." Only now, for the first time, did Vronsky take in the fact that there was a person attached to her — a husband. He had known she had a husband, but he had hardly believed in his existence, and only now fully believed in him, with his head and shoulders and his legs in black trousers — especially when he saw this husband calmly take her arm with a sense of property.

Seeing Alexey Alexandrovitch with his Petersburg face and severely self-confident figure, in his round hat with his rather prominent back, he believed in him, and felt an unpleasant sensation — the kind a man tortured by thirst might feel on reaching a spring and finding a dog, a sheep, or a pig that had drunk from it and muddied the water. Alexey Alexandrovitch's walk, with its swing of the hips and flat feet, particularly annoyed Vronsky. He could recognize in no one but himself an unquestionable right to love her. But she was still the same, and the sight of her affected him the same way, physically reviving him, stirring him, and filling his soul with rapture. He told his German valet, who ran up to him from the second class, to take his things and go on, while he himself went up to her. He saw the first meeting between husband and wife, and noted with a lover's sharpness the signs of slight reserve with which she spoke to her husband. "No, she does not love him and cannot love him," he decided to himself.
Just as he was approaching Anna Arkadyevna, he noticed with joy too that she was aware of his being near, and looked round, and seeing him, turned back to her husband.

"Did you have a good night?" he asked, bowing to her and to her husband together, and leaving it for Alexey Alexandrovitch to take the bow as meant for him too, and to acknowledge it or not, as he saw fit.
"Thank you, very good," she answered.

Her face looked tired, and there was none of that play of eagerness in it, peeping out from her smile and her eyes; but for a single instant, as she glanced at him, there was a flash of something in her eyes, and although the flash died away at once, he was happy for that moment. She glanced at her husband to see whether he knew Vronsky. Alexey Alexandrovitch looked at Vronsky with displeasure, vaguely recalling who he was. Vronsky's composure and self-confidence struck, like a scythe against a stone, the cold self-confidence of Alexey Alexandrovitch.
"Count Vronsky," said Anna.
"Ah! We're acquainted, I believe," Alexey Alexandrovitch said indifferently, holding out his hand.
"You set off with the mother and come back with the son," he said, articulating each syllable as though each one were a separate favor he was conferring.
"You're back from leave, I take it?" he said, and without waiting for an answer turned to his wife in his bantering tone: "Were a great many tears shed in Moscow at parting?"
By addressing his wife this way, he let Vronsky know that he wished to be left alone, and, turning slightly toward him, he touched his hat; but Vronsky turned to Anna Arkadyevna.
"I hope I may have the honor of calling on you," he said.
Alexey Alexandrovitch glanced with his weary eyes at Vronsky.

"Delighted," he said coolly. "Mondays we're at home. Most fortunate," he said to his wife, dismissing Vronsky entirely, "that I should have just half an hour to meet you, so I could prove my devotion," he continued in the same bantering tone.

"You put too much emphasis on your devotion for me to value it much," she replied in the same jesting tone, listening in spite of herself to the sound of Vronsky's steps behind them. "But what does it have to do with me?" she said to herself, and she began asking her husband how Seryozha had got on without her.

"Oh, splendidly! Mariette says he has been very good. And... I must disappoint you... but he hasn't missed you as your husband has. But once again _merci,_ my dear, for giving me a day. Our dear _Samovar_ will be delighted." (He used to call Countess Lidia Ivanovna, well known in society, the samovar, because she was always bubbling over with excitement.) "She has been continually asking after you. And, do you know, if I may venture to advise you, you should go see her today. You know how she takes everything to heart. Just now, with all her own cares, she's worried about getting the Oblonskys back together."
Countess Lidia Ivanovna was a friend of her husband's, and the center of one of those coteries of the Petersburg world that Anna was, through her husband, most closely connected with.
"But you know I wrote to her?"

"Still she'll want to hear the details. Go and see her, if you're not too tired, my dear. Well, Kondraty will take you in the carriage, while I go to my committee. I shan't be alone at dinner again," Alexey Alexandrovitch went on, no longer in a sarcastic tone. "You wouldn't believe how I've missed..." And, with a long pressure of her hand and a meaningful smile, he put her into her carriage.

title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: The first person to greet Anna at home was her son. He dashed down the stairs to her, ignoring the governess's call, and shrieked with desperate joy, "Mother! Mother!" Running up to her, he flung himself onto her neck.
"I told you it was mother!" he shouted to the governess. "I knew!"

And her son, like her husband, aroused in Anna a feeling akin to disappointment. She had imagined him better than he was in reality. She had to let herself drop down to reality to enjoy him as he really was. But even as he was, he was charming, with his fair curls, his blue eyes, and his plump, graceful little legs in their tightly pulled-up stockings. Anna felt an almost physical pleasure in the sense of his nearness, his caresses, and a moral comfort when she met his simple, trusting, loving gaze and heard his naïve questions. Anna took out the presents Dolly's children had sent him, and told her son what sort of little girl Tanya was in Moscow, and how Tanya could read and even teach the other children.
"Why, am I not as nice as her?" Seryozha asked.
"To me you're nicer than anyone in the world."
"I know that," said Seryozha, smiling.

Anna had not had time to drink her coffee when Countess Lidia Ivanovna was announced. Countess Lidia Ivanovna was a tall, stout woman with an unhealthily sallow complexion and splendid, pensive black eyes. Anna liked her, but today she seemed to be seeing her for the first time with all her faults.
"Well, my dear, so you took the olive branch?" Countess Lidia Ivanovna asked the moment she walked in.
"Yes, it's all over, but it was all much less serious than we'd thought," Anna answered. "My _belle-sœur_ is in general too hasty."
But Countess Lidia Ivanovna, though she took an interest in everything that didn't concern her, had a habit of never listening to what did interest her; she cut Anna off:
"Yes, there's plenty of sorrow and evil in the world. I'm so worried today."
"Oh, why?" Anna asked, trying to suppress a smile.

"I'm beginning to get tired of fighting fruitlessly for the truth, and sometimes I'm quite unhinged by it. The Society of the Little Sisters" (this was a religiously patriotic, philanthropic institution) "was going splendidly, but with these gentlemen it's impossible to do anything," Countess Lidia Ivanovna added, in a tone of ironic submission to destiny. "They pounce on the idea and distort it, and then work it out so pettily and unworthily. Two or three people, your husband among them, understand all the importance of the thing, but the others simply drag it down. Yesterday Pravdin wrote to me..."
Pravdin was a well-known Panslavist abroad, and Countess Lidia Ivanovna gave the gist of his letter.

Then the countess told her of more disagreements and intrigues against the work of the unification of the churches, and rushed off, as she had to be at the meeting of some society that day and also at the Slavonic committee.

"It was all the same before, of course; but why is it I didn't notice it before?" Anna asked herself. "Or has she been particularly irritated today? It's really ludicrous; her object is doing good; she's a Christian, yet she's always angry; and she always has enemies, and always enemies in the name of Christianity and doing good."

After Countess Lidia Ivanovna another friend came, the wife of a chief secretary, who told her all the news of the town. At three o'clock she too went away, promising to come for dinner. Alexey Alexandrovitch was at the ministry. Anna, left alone, spent the time till dinner attending to her son's meal (he ate apart from his parents), putting her things in order, and reading and answering the notes and letters that had piled up on her table.
The feeling of causeless shame she had felt on the train, and her excitement too, had vanished completely. Back in the familiar conditions of her life, she felt resolute and beyond reproach again.

She remembered with wonder her state of mind the day before. "What was it? Nothing. Vronsky said something silly, which was easy to put a stop to, and I answered the way I should have. To speak of it to my husband would be unnecessary and out of the question. To speak of it would be to attach importance to something that has none." She remembered how she had told her husband of what was almost a declaration made to her in Petersburg by a young man, one of her husband's subordinates, and how Alexey Alexandrovitch had answered that every woman living in the world is exposed to such incidents, but that he had the fullest confidence in her tact and could never lower her and himself by jealousy. "So then there's no reason to speak of it. And indeed, thank God, there's nothing to speak of," she told herself.

title: Chapter 34
paragraphs: When Vronsky went from Petersburg to Moscow, he had left his large set of rooms in Morskaia to his friend and favorite comrade Petritsky.

Petritsky was a young lieutenant, not particularly well-connected, and not just not wealthy but always hopelessly in debt. Toward evening he was always drunk, and he had often been locked up after all kinds of ludicrous and disgraceful scandals, but he was a favorite of both his comrades and his superior officers. Arriving at twelve o'clock from the station at his flat, Vronsky saw a familiar hired carriage at the outer door. While he was still outside his own door, as he rang, he heard masculine laughter, the lisp of a feminine voice, and Petritsky's voice: "If that's one of the villains, don't let him in!" Vronsky told the servant not to announce him and slipped quietly into the first room. Baroness Shilton, a friend of Petritsky's, with a rosy little face and flaxen hair, resplendent in a lilac satin gown and filling the whole room like a canary with her Parisian chatter, sat at the round table making coffee. Petritsky, in his overcoat, and the cavalry captain Kamerovsky, in full uniform, probably just come from duty, were sitting on either side of her.

"Bravo, Vronsky!" Petritsky shouted, jumping up and scraping his chair. "Our host himself! Baroness, some coffee for him out of the new coffee pot. Why, we didn't expect you! I hope you're satisfied with the ornament of your study," he said, indicating the baroness. "You know each other, of course?"
"I should think so," Vronsky said with a bright smile, pressing the baroness's little hand. "What next! I'm an old friend."
"You're home from a journey," said the baroness, "so I'm off. Oh, I'll be off this minute, if I'm in the way."
"You're at home wherever you are, baroness," said Vronsky. "How do you do, Kamerovsky?" he added, coolly shaking hands with Kamerovsky.
"There — you never know how to say such pretty things," the baroness said, turning to Petritsky.
"No, what's that for? After dinner I say things every bit as good."

"There's no credit in them after dinner. Well then, I'll make you some coffee, so go and wash and get ready," the baroness said, sitting down again and anxiously turning the screw on the new coffee pot. "Pierre, hand me the coffee," she said to Petritsky, whom she called Pierre as a contraction of his surname, making no secret of her relations with him. "I'll put it in."
"You'll spoil it!"
"No, I won't spoil it! Well, and your wife?" the baroness asked suddenly, interrupting Vronsky's conversation with his comrade. "We've been marrying you off here. Did you bring your wife?"
"No, baroness. I was born a Bohemian, and a Bohemian I shall die."
"So much the better, so much the better. Shake hands on it."
And the baroness, holding on to Vronsky, began telling him, with many jokes, about her latest new plans for life, asking his advice.

"He persists in refusing to give me a divorce! Well, what am I to do?" (_He_ was her husband.) "Now I want to bring a suit against him. What do you advise? Kamerovsky, watch the coffee — it's boiling over. You see, I'm engrossed with business! I want a lawsuit, because I have to have my property. Do you see the folly of it? On the pretext of my being unfaithful to him," she said contemptuously, "he wants to get hold of my fortune."

Vronsky listened with pleasure to this light-hearted prattle of a pretty woman, agreed with her, gave her half-joking advice, and altogether dropped at once into the tone he habitually took with such women. In his Petersburg world all people were divided into two utterly opposed classes. One, the lower class — vulgar, stupid, and above all ridiculous people — believed that one husband ought to live with the one wife he had lawfully married; that a girl should be innocent, a woman modest, and a man manly, self-controlled, and strong; that one ought to bring up one's children, earn one's bread, and pay one's debts; and various similar absurdities. This was the class of old-fashioned and ridiculous people. But there was another class, the real people. To this class they all belonged, and in it the great thing was to be elegant, generous, plucky, gay, to throw oneself without a blush into every passion, and to laugh at everything else.

Only for the first moment was Vronsky startled by the impression of a quite different world that he had brought with him from Moscow. But immediately, as if slipping his feet into old slippers, he sank back into the light-hearted, pleasant world he had always lived in.

The coffee never really got made, but spluttered over everyone, and boiled away, doing exactly what was required of it — that is, producing plenty of cause for noise and laughter, and spoiling a costly rug and the baroness's gown.
"Well now, good-bye, or you'll never finish washing, and the worst sin a gentleman can commit will be on my conscience. So your advice is to put a knife to his throat?"
"To be sure, and arrange for your hand not to be far from his lips. He'll kiss your hand, and all will end satisfactorily," answered Vronsky.
"So at the Français, then!" and, with a rustle of her skirts, she vanished.
Kamerovsky got up too, and Vronsky, without waiting for him to leave, shook hands and went off to his dressing-room.

While he was washing, Petritsky described to him in brief outlines his situation as it had changed since Vronsky had left Petersburg. No money at all. His father had said he wouldn't give him any and wouldn't pay his debts. His tailor was trying to get him locked up, and another fellow was threatening the same. The colonel of the regiment had announced that if these scandals didn't stop he'd have to leave. As for the baroness, he was sick to death of her, especially since she'd started constantly offering to lend him money. But he had found a girl — he'd show her to Vronsky — a marvel, exquisite, in the strict Oriental style, "genre of the slave Rebecca, don't you know." He'd had a row, too, with Berkoshov, and was going to send seconds to him, but of course it would come to nothing. Altogether everything was supremely amusing and jolly. And, not letting his comrade go into further details, Petritsky went on to tell him all the interesting news. As he listened to Petritsky's familiar stories in the familiar setting of the rooms he had spent the last three years in, Vronsky felt a delightful sense of coming back to the careless Petersburg life he was used to.
