"Impossible!" he cried, letting down the pedal of the washbasin in which he had been dousing his healthy red neck. "Impossible!" he cried at the news that Laura had thrown over Fertinghof and made up to Mileev. "And is he as stupid and pleased as ever? Well, and how's Buzulukov?"

"Oh, there's a tale about Buzulukov — simply lovely!" cried Petritsky. "You know his weakness for balls — he never misses a single court ball. He went to a big ball in a new helmet. Have you seen the new helmets? Very nice, lighter. Well, so he's standing... No, listen, do listen."
"I am listening," answered Vronsky, rubbing himself with a rough towel.

"Up comes the Grand Duchess with some ambassador or other, and, as ill-luck would have it, she starts talking to him about the new helmets. The Grand Duchess positively wanted to show the new helmet to the ambassador. They see our friend standing there." (Petritsky mimicked how he was standing with the helmet.) "The Grand Duchess asked him to give her the helmet; he doesn't give it to her. What do you think of that? Well, everyone's winking at him, nodding, frowning — give it to her, do! He doesn't give it to her. He's mute as a fish. Only picture it!... Well, the... whatsisname, whatever he was... tries to take the helmet from him... he won't give it up! He pulls it from him and hands it to the Grand Duchess. 'Here, your Highness,' says he, 'is the new helmet.' She turned the helmet the other side up, and — just picture it! — plop went a pear and sweetmeats out of it, two pounds of sweetmeats!... He'd been storing them up, the darling!"

Vronsky burst into roars of laughter. And long afterwards, when he was talking about other things, he broke into his healthy laugh again, showing his strong, close rows of teeth, whenever the thought of the helmet came back to him.

Having heard all the news, Vronsky, with his valet's help, got into his uniform and went off to report for duty. After that, he meant to drive to his brother's and then to Betsy's, and to make a few other calls so as to start moving in the circles where he might run into Madame Karenina. As he always did in Petersburg, he left home not meaning to return till late at night.
PART TWO

title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: At the end of the winter, in the Shtcherbatskys' house, a consultation was being held that was to pronounce on the state of Kitty's health and the measures to be taken to restore her failing strength. She had been ill, and as spring came on she grew worse. The family doctor gave her cod-liver oil, then iron, then nitrate of silver, but as the first and the second and the third all did no good, and as his advice when spring came was to go abroad, a celebrated physician was called in. The celebrated physician, a very handsome man, still youngish, asked to examine the patient. He maintained, with a peculiar satisfaction, it seemed, that maidenly modesty is a mere relic of barbarism, and that nothing could be more natural than for a man still youngish to handle a young girl naked. He thought it natural because he did it every day, and felt and thought, as it seemed to him, no harm as he did it, and consequently he regarded modesty in the girl not merely as a relic of barbarism, but also as an insult to himself.

There was nothing for it but to submit. Though all the doctors had been at the same school, read the same books, and learned the same science, and though some people said this celebrated doctor was actually a bad one, in the princess's household and circle it had somehow been accepted that this celebrated doctor alone had some special knowledge, and that he alone could save Kitty. After a careful examination and sounding of the bewildered patient — who was dazed with shame — the celebrated doctor, having scrupulously washed his hands, stood in the drawing-room talking to the prince. The prince frowned and coughed as he listened. As a man who had seen something of life, no fool and no invalid, he had no faith in medicine, and in his heart was furious at the whole farce, especially since he was perhaps the only one who fully grasped the cause of Kitty's illness. "Conceited blockhead," he thought, listening to the celebrated doctor's chatter about his daughter's symptoms. The doctor, meanwhile, was barely managing to restrain his contempt for this old gentleman, and barely managing to condescend to the level of his intelligence. He could see that talking to the old man was pointless, and that the principal person in the house was the mother. Before her he had decided to cast his pearls. At that moment the princess came into the drawing-room with the family doctor. The prince withdrew, trying not to show how ridiculous he thought the whole performance. The princess was at her wits' end, and did not know what to do. She felt she had sinned against Kitty.
"Well, doctor, decide our fate," the princess said. "Tell me everything."
"Is there hope?" she meant to say, but her lips quivered and she could not utter the question. "Well, doctor?"
"In a moment, princess. I'll talk it over with my colleague, and then I'll have the honor of laying my opinion before you."
"So we had better leave you?"
"As you please."
The princess went out with a sigh.

When the doctors were left alone, the family doctor began timidly explaining his opinion, that there was a beginning of tuberculous trouble, but... and so on. The celebrated doctor listened to him, and in the middle of his sentence looked at his big gold watch.
"Yes," he said. "But..."
The family doctor respectfully stopped in the middle of his observations.

"The beginning of the tuberculous process we are not, as you know, able to define; until there are cavities, there is nothing definite. But we may suspect it. And there are indications: malnutrition, nervous excitability, and so on. The question stands thus: in the presence of indications of a tuberculous process, what is to be done to maintain nutrition?"
"But, you know, there are always moral, spiritual causes at the bottom of these cases," the family doctor allowed himself to interpolate with a subtle smile.

"Yes, that goes without saying," the celebrated physician answered, glancing again at his watch. "Beg pardon, is the Yausky bridge done yet, or will I have to drive round?" he asked. "Ah! It is. Oh well, then I can do it in twenty minutes. So we were saying the problem may be put thus: to maintain nutrition and tone up the nerves. The one is in close connection with the other; one must attack both sides at once."
"And how about a tour abroad?" the family doctor asked.

"I've no liking for foreign tours. And take note: if there is an early stage of tuberculous process, of which we can't be certain, a foreign tour will be of no use. What is wanted is means for improving nutrition, not lowering it." And the celebrated doctor expounded his treatment plan with Soden waters, a remedy obviously prescribed primarily on the grounds that it could do no harm.
The family doctor listened attentively and respectfully.
"But in favor of a foreign trip I would press the change of habits, the removal from surroundings that call up memories. And then the mother wishes it," he added.
"Ah! In that case, to be sure, let them go. Only, those German quacks are mischievous... They'll have to be talked round... Well, let them go, then."
He glanced once more at his watch.
"Oh, time's up already." And he made for the door. The celebrated doctor announced to the princess (a sense of what was due from him made him do it) that he ought to see the patient once more.
"What! Another examination?" the mother cried, with horror.
"Oh, no, only a few details, princess."
"Come this way."

And the mother, accompanied by the doctor, went into the drawing-room to Kitty. Wasted and flushed, with a peculiar glitter in her eyes — left there by the agony of shame she had just been put through — Kitty was standing in the middle of the room. When the doctor came in she flushed crimson, and her eyes filled with tears. All her illness and treatment struck her as so stupid, ludicrous even! Doctoring her seemed to her as absurd as putting together the pieces of a broken vase. Her heart was broken. Why were they trying to cure her with pills and powders? But she could not grieve her mother, especially as her mother considered herself to blame.
"May I trouble you to sit down, princess?" the celebrated doctor said to her.
He sat down with a smile, facing her, took her pulse, and again began putting his tiresome questions to her. She answered him, and all at once stood up, furious.
"Excuse me, doctor, but there's really no point in this. This is the third time you've asked me the same thing."
The celebrated doctor was not offended.
"Nervous irritability," he said to the princess when Kitty had left the room. "However, I had finished..."

And the doctor began scientifically explaining to the princess, as an exceptionally intelligent woman, the condition of the young princess, and concluded by insisting on drinking the waters, which were certainly harmless. To the question whether they should go abroad, the doctor plunged into deep meditation, as if resolving a weighty problem. Finally his decision was pronounced: they were to go abroad, but to put no faith in foreign quacks, and to apply to him in any need.

It was as if some piece of good fortune had come about once the doctor had gone. The mother was much more cheerful when she went back to her daughter, and Kitty pretended to be more cheerful. She had often, almost always, to be pretending now.
"Really, mamma, I'm quite well. But if you want to go abroad, then let's go!" she said, and trying to seem interested in the proposed trip, she began talking about preparations for the journey.

title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Soon after the doctor, Dolly arrived. She knew a consultation was to take place that day, and although she was only just up after her confinement (she had had another baby, a little girl, born at the end of the winter), and although she had trouble and anxiety enough of her own, she had left her tiny baby and a sick child behind to come and hear Kitty's fate, which was to be decided that day.
"Well, well?" she said, coming into the drawing-room without taking off her hat. "You're all in good spirits. Good news, then?"

They tried to tell her what the doctor had said, but it turned out that although the doctor had talked distinctly enough and at great length, it was utterly impossible to report what he had said. The only point of real interest was that it was settled they would go abroad.

Dolly could not help sighing. Her dearest friend, her sister, was going away. And her own life was not a cheerful one. Her relations with Stepan Arkadyevitch after their reconciliation had become humiliating. The union Anna had cemented turned out to be of no solid character, and family harmony was breaking down again at the same point. There had been nothing definite, but Stepan Arkadyevitch was hardly ever at home; money, too, was hardly ever forthcoming, and Dolly was continually tortured by suspicions of infidelity, which she tried to dismiss, dreading the agonies of jealousy she had already been through. The first onslaught of jealousy, once lived through, could never come again, and even the discovery of infidelities could not affect her now as it had the first time. Such a discovery now would only mean breaking up family habits, and she let herself be deceived, despising him and still more herself, for the weakness. Besides this, the care of her large family was a constant worry to her: first, the nursing of her young baby was not going well, then the nurse had gone away, now one of the children had fallen ill.
"Well, how are all of you?" her mother asked.

"Ah, mamma, we have plenty of troubles of our own. Lili is ill, and I'm afraid it's scarlatina. I came here now to hear about Kitty, and then I'll shut myself up entirely, if — God forbid — it really is scarlatina."
After the doctor's departure, the old prince came in too from his study, and after presenting his cheek to Dolly and exchanging a few words with her, he turned to his wife.
"How have you settled it? You're going? Well, and what do you mean to do with me?"
"I suppose you had better stay here, Alexander," said his wife.
"That's as you like."
"Mamma, why shouldn't father come with us?" said Kitty. "It would be nicer for him and for us too."

The old prince got up and stroked Kitty's hair. She lifted her head and looked at him with a forced smile. It always seemed to her that he understood her better than anyone in the family, though he did not say much about her. Being the youngest, she was her father's favorite, and she fancied that his love gave him insight. When now her glance met his blue, kindly eyes looking intently at her, it seemed to her that he saw right through her, and understood all the bad things going on inside her. Reddening, she stretched out toward him, expecting a kiss, but he only patted her hair and said:
"These stupid chignons! You can't get at the real daughter. One simply strokes the bristles of dead women. Well, Dolinka," he turned to his elder daughter, "what's your young buck up to, hey?"
"Nothing, father," Dolly answered, understanding her husband was meant. "He's always out. I hardly ever lay eyes on him," she could not help adding with a sarcastic smile.
"Why, hasn't he gone to the country yet — to see about selling that forest?"
"No, he's still getting ready for the journey."

"Oh, that's it!" the prince said. "And so I'm to be getting ready for a journey too? At your service," he said to his wife, sitting down. "And I'll tell you what, Katia," he went on to his younger daughter, "you must wake up one fine day and say to yourself: Why, I'm quite well, and merry, and going out again with father for an early morning walk in the frost. Eh?"

What her father said sounded simple enough, yet at these words Kitty became confused and overwhelmed like a criminal caught in the act. "Yes, he sees it all, he understands it all, and in these words he's telling me that, ashamed though I may be, I have to get over my shame." She could not summon the spirit to make any answer. She tried to begin, and all at once burst into tears and rushed out of the room.
"See what comes of your jokes!" the princess pounced down on her husband. "You're always..." she started in on a string of reproaches.
The prince listened to the princess's scolding rather a long while without speaking, but his face grew more and more frowning.

"She's so much to be pitied, poor child, so much to be pitied, and you don't feel how it hurts her to hear the slightest reference to the cause of it. Ah! To be so mistaken in people!" said the princess, and by the change in her tone both Dolly and the prince knew she was speaking of Vronsky. "I don't know why there aren't laws against such base, dishonorable people."

"Ah, I can't bear to hear you!" the prince said gloomily, getting up from his low chair and seeming anxious to get away, yet stopping in the doorway. "There are laws, madam, and since you've challenged me to it, I'll tell you who's to blame for it all — you, you and no one else. There have always been, and there still are, laws against such young gallants! Yes — if there had been nothing that ought not to have been, old as I am, I'd have called him out to the barrier, the young dandy. Yes, and now you physic her and call in these quacks."
The prince clearly had plenty more to say, but the instant the princess heard his tone she gave way at once and became penitent, as she always did on serious occasions.
"Alexander, Alexander," she whispered, moving toward him and beginning to weep.
As soon as she began to cry the prince calmed down too. He went over to her.

"There, that's enough, that's enough! You're wretched too, I know. It can't be helped. There's no great harm done. God is merciful... thanks..." he said, not knowing what he was saying, as he responded to the tearful kiss the princess pressed onto his hand. And the prince left the room.

Before this, the moment Kitty had gone out of the room in tears, Dolly, with her motherly, family instincts, had promptly seen that here a woman's work lay before her, and had prepared to do it. She took off her hat and, morally speaking, rolled up her sleeves and prepared for action. While her mother was attacking her father, she tried to restrain her, so far as filial respect would allow. During the prince's outburst she was silent; she felt ashamed for her mother, and tender toward her father for so quickly being kind again. But when her father left them, she made ready for what was the chief thing needed — to go to Kitty and console her.
"I've been meaning to tell you something for a long time, mamma — did you know that Levin meant to propose to Kitty when he was here last? He told Stiva so."
"Well, what then? I don't understand..."
"So Kitty perhaps refused him? She didn't tell you?"
"No, she's said nothing to me about one or the other; she's too proud. But I know it's all because of the other one."
"Yes, but suppose she refused Levin — and she would not have refused him if it had not been for the other one, I know it. And then he deceived her so horribly."
It was too terrible for the princess to think how she had sinned against her daughter, and she broke out angrily.
"Oh, I really don't understand! Nowadays they all go their own way, and mothers haven't a word to say in anything, and then..."
"Mamma, I'll go up to her."
"Well, do. Did I tell you not to?" her mother said.

title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: When she went into Kitty's little room — a pretty, pink little room full of knick-knacks in _vieux saxe,_ as fresh, pink, white, and gay as Kitty herself had been two months earlier — Dolly remembered how they had decorated the room together the year before, with what love and gaiety. Her heart turned cold when she saw Kitty sitting on a low chair near the door, her eyes fixed unmoving on a corner of the rug. Kitty glanced at her sister, and the cold, rather ill-tempered expression on her face did not change.
"I'm just going now, and I'll have to stay shut in and you won't be able to come and see me," said Dolly, sitting down beside her. "I want to talk to you."
"What about?" Kitty asked quickly, lifting her head in alarm.
"What should it be, but your trouble?"
"I have no trouble."
"Nonsense, Kitty. Do you think I could fail to know? I know it all. And believe me, it amounts to so little... Each of us has been through it."
Kitty did not speak, and her face had a stern expression.
"He isn't worth your grieving over him," Darya Alexandrovna went on, coming straight to the point.
"No, because he's treated me with contempt," Kitty said, in a breaking voice. "Don't talk about it! Please, don't talk about it!"
"But who could have told you that? No one said that. I'm certain he was in love with you, and would still be in love with you, if it hadn't..."

"Oh, the most awful thing for me is all this sympathizing!" Kitty shrieked, suddenly flying into a passion. She turned round on her chair, flushed crimson, and, rapidly moving her fingers, pinched the clasp of her belt first with one hand and then with the other. Dolly knew this trick her sister had of clenching her hands when she was very excited; she knew, too, that in moments of excitement Kitty was capable of forgetting herself and saying a great deal too much, and Dolly would have soothed her, but it was too late.

"What, what is it you want to make me feel, eh?" Kitty said rapidly. "That I've been in love with a man who didn't care a straw for me, and that I'm dying of love for him? And this is said to me by my own sister, who imagines that... that... that she's sympathizing with me!... I don't want these condolences and humbug!"
"Kitty, you're being unfair."
"Why are you tormenting me?"
"But I... quite the contrary... I see you're unhappy..."
But Kitty in her fury did not hear her.
"I've nothing to grieve over or be comforted about. I am too proud ever to let myself care for a man who doesn't love me."
"Yes, I'm not saying that either... Only one thing. Tell me the truth," said Darya Alexandrovna, taking her by the hand. "Tell me — did Levin speak to you?"

The mention of Levin's name seemed to strip Kitty of the last remnant of self-control. She leaped up from her chair, and flinging her clasp on the ground, she gesticulated rapidly with her hands and said:

"Why bring Levin into this too? I don't understand what you're trying to torture me about. I've told you, and I'll say it again: I have some pride, and never, _never_ would I do what you're doing — go back to a man who has deceived you, who has loved another woman. I can't understand it! You can — I cannot!"

And, having said this, she glanced at her sister, and seeing that Dolly sat silent with her head sadly bowed, Kitty — instead of running out of the room as she had meant to — sat down near the door and hid her face in her handkerchief.

The silence lasted for two minutes: Dolly was thinking of herself. That humiliation she was always aware of came back to her with a special bitterness when her sister reminded her of it. She had not looked for such cruelty in her sister, and she was angry with her. But suddenly she heard the rustle of a skirt, and with it the sound of heart-rending, smothered sobbing, and felt arms about her neck. Kitty was on her knees before her.
"Dolinka, I'm so, so wretched!" she whispered penitently. And the sweet face, covered with tears, hid itself in Darya Alexandrovna's skirt.

As though tears were the indispensable oil without which the machinery of mutual confidence could not run smoothly between the two sisters, after their tears the sisters talked, not of what was uppermost in their minds, but, though they spoke of outside matters, they understood each other. Kitty knew that the words she had uttered in anger about her husband's infidelity and her humiliating position had cut her poor sister to the heart, but that she had forgiven her. Dolly for her part knew everything she had wanted to find out. She felt certain that her surmises were correct: that Kitty's misery, her inconsolable misery, was due precisely to the fact that Levin had proposed and she had refused him, and Vronsky had deceived her, and that she was fully ready to love Levin and to detest Vronsky. Kitty said not a word of that; she talked of nothing but her spiritual condition.

"I have nothing to make me miserable," she said, calming down. "But can you understand that everything has become hateful, loathsome, coarse to me, and I myself most of all? You can't imagine the loathsome thoughts I have about everything."
"Why, what loathsome thoughts can you have?" Dolly asked, smiling.

"The most utterly loathsome and coarse — I can't tell you. It's not unhappiness, or low spirits, but much worse. As if everything that was good in me was all hidden away, and nothing was left but the most loathsome. Now, how am I to tell you?" she went on, seeing the puzzled look in her sister's eyes. "Father just now began saying something to me... It seems to me he thinks all I want is to be married. Mother takes me to a ball: it seems to me she only takes me to get me married off as soon as may be, and be rid of me. I know it's not the truth, but I can't drive away such thoughts. Eligible suitors, as they call them — I can't bear to see them. It seems to me they're taking stock of me and summing me up. In the old days going anywhere in a ball dress was a simple joy to me, I admired myself; now I feel ashamed and awkward. And then! The doctor... Then..." Kitty hesitated; she wanted to add that ever since the change had taken place in her, Stepan Arkadyevitch had become unbearably repulsive to her, and that she could not look at him without the grossest, most hideous conceptions rising before her imagination.
"Oh well, everything presents itself to me in the coarsest, most loathsome light," she went on. "That's my illness. Perhaps it will pass."
"But you mustn't think about it."
"I can't help it. I'm never happy except with the children at your house."
"What a pity you can't be with me!"
"Oh, yes, I'm coming. I've had scarlatina, and I'll persuade mamma to let me."

Kitty insisted on having her way and went to stay with her sister and nursed the children all through the scarlatina, for scarlatina it turned out to be. The two sisters brought all six children safely through it, but Kitty was no better in health, and in Lent the Shtcherbatskys went abroad.

title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: The highest Petersburg society is essentially one: in it everyone knows everyone else, and everyone even visits everyone else. But within this great set there are subdivisions. Anna Arkadyevna Karenina had friends and close ties in three different circles of this highest society. One was her husband's government-official set, consisting of his colleagues and subordinates, brought together in the most varied and capricious manner and belonging to different social strata. Anna now found it hard to remember the feeling of almost awe-struck reverence she had at first felt for these people. Now she knew them all the way people know one another in a country town: she knew their habits and weaknesses, knew where the shoe pinched each of them. She knew their relations with one another and with the head authorities, knew who was on whose side, how each kept his position, where they agreed and disagreed. But the circle of political, masculine interests had never interested her, despite Countess Lidia Ivanovna's influence, and she avoided it.

Another little set with which Anna was on close terms was the one through which Alexey Alexandrovitch had made his career. The center of this circle was Countess Lidia Ivanovna. It was a group made up of elderly, ugly, benevolent, godly women, and clever, learned, ambitious men. One of the clever men belonging to it had called it "the conscience of Petersburg society." Alexey Alexandrovitch had the highest esteem for this circle, and Anna, with her special gift for getting on with everyone, had in the early days of her life in Petersburg made friends in it too. Now, since her return from Moscow, she had come to find this set insufferable. It seemed to her that both she and all of them were insincere, and she felt so bored and ill at ease in that world that she went to see Countess Lidia Ivanovna as little as possible.

The third circle Anna had ties to was preeminently the fashionable world — the world of balls, of dinners, of sumptuous dresses, the world that clung to the court with one hand so as not to sink to the level of the demi-monde. The demi-monde itself the members of that fashionable world believed they despised, though their tastes were not merely similar but in fact identical. Anna's connection with this circle was maintained through Princess Betsy Tverskaya, her cousin's wife, who had an income of a hundred and twenty thousand roubles and had taken a great fancy to Anna ever since her debut, showering her with attention and drawing her into her set, making fun of Countess Lidia Ivanovna's coterie.
"When I'm old and ugly I'll be the same," Betsy used to say; "but for a pretty young woman like you it's too early to enter that charitable institution."

Anna had at first avoided Princess Tverskaya's world as much as she could, because it required an expenditure beyond her means, and besides, in her heart she preferred the first circle. But ever since her trip to Moscow she had done the opposite. She avoided her serious-minded friends and ventured out into the fashionable world. There she met Vronsky, and felt a thrilling joy at those meetings. She met Vronsky particularly often at Betsy's, since Betsy was a Vronsky by birth and his cousin. Vronsky was everywhere he had any chance of meeting Anna and speaking to her, when he could, of his love. She gave him no encouragement, but every time she met him there welled up in her heart that same feeling of quickened life that had come over her that day on the train when she had first seen him. She was aware that her delight sparkled in her eyes and curved her lips into a smile, and she could not extinguish the look of that delight.

At first Anna sincerely believed she was displeased with him for daring to pursue her. Soon after her return from Moscow, arriving at a _soirée_ where she had expected to meet him and finding he was not there, she realized clearly, by the rush of disappointment, that she had been deceiving herself, and that this pursuit was not merely not distasteful to her — it had become the whole interest of her life.

The celebrated singer was singing for the second time, and all of fashionable society was in the theater. Vronsky, seeing his cousin from his seat in the front row, did not wait till the _entr'acte_, but went to her box.

"Why didn't you come to dinner?" she said to him. "I'm amazed at the second sight of lovers," she added with a smile so quiet that only he could hear; "_she wasn't there_. But come back after the opera."
Vronsky looked at her questioningly. She nodded. He thanked her with a smile and sat down beside her.

"But how well I remember your jeers!" Princess Betsy went on, taking a particular pleasure in following this passion through to a successful issue. "What's become of all that? You're caught, my dear boy."
"That's my one wish, to be caught," Vronsky answered with his serene, good-humored smile. "If I have any complaint, it's that I'm not caught enough, to tell the truth. I'm beginning to lose hope."

"Why, whatever hope could you have?" said Betsy, offended on behalf of her friend. "_Entendons nous_..." But in her eyes there were gleams of light that betrayed she understood, just as precisely as he did, what hope he might have.

"None whatsoever," said Vronsky, laughing and showing his even rows of teeth. "Excuse me," he added, taking an opera-glass from her hand and proceeding to scan, over her bare shoulder, the row of boxes facing them. "I'm afraid I'm becoming ridiculous."

He was very well aware that he ran no risk of looking ridiculous in the eyes of Betsy or any other fashionable people. He was very well aware that in their eyes the position of an unsuccessful lover of a young girl, or of any woman free to marry, might be ridiculous. But the position of a man pursuing a married woman, and, regardless of everything else, staking his life on drawing her into adultery, had something fine and grand about it, and could never be ridiculous; and so it was with a proud, gay smile under his mustaches that he lowered the opera-glass and looked at his cousin.
"But why didn't you come to dinner?" she asked, admiring him.

"I have to tell you about that. I was busy — and doing what, do you suppose? Give yourself a hundred guesses, a thousand... you'd never guess. I've been reconciling a husband with a man who had insulted his wife. Yes, really."
"Well, did you succeed?"
"Almost."
"You really must tell me about it," she said, getting up. "Come to me in the next _entr'acte_."
"I can't; I'm going to the French theater."
"Away from Nilsson?" Betsy asked, horrified, though she herself couldn't have told Nilsson's voice from any chorus girl's.
"Can't help it. I have an appointment there, all to do with my mission of peace."

"'Blessed are the peacemakers; theirs is the kingdom of heaven,'" said Betsy, vaguely recalling having heard some such saying from someone. "Very well, then; sit down and tell me what it's all about."
And she sat down again.

title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: "This is a bit indiscreet, but it's so good there's an awful temptation to tell the story," said Vronsky, looking at her with his laughing eyes. "I'm not going to name names."
"But I'll guess, so much the better."
"Well, listen: two festive young men were driving —"
"Officers from your regiment, of course?"
"I didn't say they were officers — two young men who had been lunching."
"In other words, drinking."

"Possibly. They were driving on their way to dinner at a friend's, in the most festive state of mind. They catch sight of a pretty woman in a hired sledge; she overtakes them, looks back, and, so they fancy, nods and laughs at them. They follow her, of course. They gallop at full speed. To their amazement, the fair one alights at the entrance of the very house they were going to. The fair one darts upstairs to the top floor. They get a glimpse of red lips beneath a short veil, and exquisite little feet."
"You describe it with such feeling I suspect you must be one of the two."

"And after what you just said! Well, the young men go in to their comrade's; he was giving a farewell dinner. There they certainly did drink a little too much, as one always does at farewell dinners. And at dinner they inquire who lives at the top of that house. No one knows; only their host's valet, in answer to their question whether any 'young ladies' lived on the top floor, said that there were a great many of them about the area. After dinner the two young men go into their host's study and write a letter to the unknown fair one. They compose an ardent epistle, a declaration in fact, and carry the letter upstairs themselves, so as to clear up anything in it that might not be perfectly clear."
"Why are you telling me these horrible stories? Well?"

"They ring. A maid opens the door, they hand her the letter and assure her that they're both so in love they'll die on the spot at the door. The maid, stupefied, takes their messages inside. All at once a gentleman appears with whiskers like sausages, as red as a lobster, announces that no one lives in the flat except his wife, and sends them both about their business."
"How do you know he had whiskers like sausages, as you say?"
"Ah, you shall hear. I've just been to make peace between them."
"Well, and what then?"

"That's the most interesting part of the story. It turns out it's a happy couple, a government clerk and his lady. The government clerk files a complaint, and I became the mediator — and what a mediator! I assure you, Talleyrand couldn't hold a candle to me."
"Why, where was the difficulty?"

"Ah, you shall hear... We apologize in due form: we are in despair, we beg forgiveness for the unfortunate misunderstanding. The government clerk with the sausages begins to melt, but he, too, wants to express his sentiments, and the moment he begins to express them, he begins to get hot and say nasty things, and once again I have to trot out all my diplomatic talents. I conceded that their conduct was bad, but I urged him to take into account their heedlessness, their youth; and then, too, the young men had only just been lunching together. 'You understand. They regret it deeply, and beg you to overlook their misbehavior.' The government clerk softened once more. 'I consent, count, and am ready to overlook it; but you understand my wife — my wife is a respectable woman — has been exposed to the persecution and insults and effrontery of young upstarts, scoundrels...' And, you must understand, the young upstarts are present the whole time, and I have to keep the peace between them. Again I call on all my diplomacy, and again, just as the thing was about to be over, our friend the government clerk gets hot and red, and his sausages stand on end with wrath, and once more I launch into diplomatic wiles."
"Ah, he must tell you this story!" Betsy said, laughing, to a lady who came into her box. "He has been making me laugh so."

"Well, _bonne chance_!" she added, giving Vronsky one finger of the hand in which she held her fan, and with a shrug of her shoulders she twitched down the bodice of her gown that had worked up, so as to be duly bare as she moved forward toward the footlights into the light of the gas, and the gaze of every eye.

Vronsky drove to the French theater, where he really did have to see the colonel of his regiment, who never missed a single performance there. He wanted to see him to report on the result of his mediation, which had occupied and amused him for the last three days. Petritsky, whom he liked, was implicated in the affair, and the other culprit was a capital fellow and first-rate comrade who had lately joined the regiment, the young Prince Kedrov. And what was most important, the interests of the regiment were involved as well.

Both young men were in Vronsky's company. The colonel of the regiment was waited on by the government clerk, Venden, with a complaint against his officers, who had insulted his wife. His young wife — so Venden told the story (he had been married half a year) — was at church with her mother and, suddenly overcome by indisposition arising from her interesting condition, could not remain standing, and drove home in the first sledge, a smart-looking one, she came across. On the spot the officers set off in pursuit of her; she was alarmed, and feeling still worse, ran upstairs home. Venden himself, returning from his office, heard a ring at the bell and voices, went out, and, seeing the intoxicated officers with a letter, turned them out. He demanded exemplary punishment.

"Yes, it's all very well," the colonel said to Vronsky, whom he had invited to come see him. "Petritsky is becoming impossible. Not a week goes by without some scandal. This government clerk won't let it drop — he'll keep at it."

Vronsky saw all the thanklessness of the business, and that there could be no question of a duel, that everything had to be done to soften the government clerk and hush the matter up. The colonel had called Vronsky in precisely because he knew him to be an honorable and intelligent man, and above all a man who cared for the honor of the regiment. They talked it over and decided that Petritsky and Kedrov must go with Vronsky to Venden's to apologize. The colonel and Vronsky were both fully aware that Vronsky's name and rank would contribute greatly to softening the injured husband's feelings.
And these two influences were not, in fact, without effect; though the result remained, as Vronsky had described, uncertain.

Once at the French theater, Vronsky withdrew with the colonel to the foyer and reported his success — or non-success. The colonel, thinking it all over, decided not to pursue the matter further, but then, for his own satisfaction, proceeded to cross-examine Vronsky about his interview; and it was a long while before he could restrain his laughter as Vronsky described how the government clerk, after subsiding for a while, would suddenly flare up again as he recalled the details, and how Vronsky, at the last half-word of conciliation, skillfully manoeuvered a retreat, shoving Petritsky out ahead of him.

"It's a disgraceful story, but killing. Kedrov really can't fight the gentleman! So he was awfully hot, was he?" he commented, laughing. "But what do you say to Claire today? She's marvelous," he went on, speaking of a new French actress. "However often you see her, she's different every day. Only the French can do that."

title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Princess Betsy drove home from the theater without waiting for the end of the last act. She had only just had time to go to her dressing-room, sprinkle her long, pale face with powder, rub it, set her dress to rights, and order tea in the big drawing-room, when one after another carriages drove up to her huge house on Bolshaya Morskaya. Her guests stepped out at the wide entrance, and the stout porter, who used to read newspapers in the mornings behind the glass door, to the edification of passers-by, noiselessly opened the immense door, letting the visitors past him into the house.

Almost at the same instant the hostess, her coiffure freshly arranged and her face refreshed, walked in at one door, and her guests at the other door of the drawing-room — a large room with dark walls, downy rugs, and a brightly lit table gleaming with candles, white cloth, a silver samovar, and transparent china tea-things.

The hostess sat down at the table and took off her gloves. Chairs were set in place with the help of footmen moving almost imperceptibly around the room; the party settled down and divided into two groups: one round the samovar near the hostess, the other at the opposite end of the drawing-room, around the handsome wife of an ambassador, in black velvet, with sharply defined black eyebrows. In both groups conversation wavered, as it always does for the first few minutes, broken up by greetings, offers of tea, and a kind of feeling-about for something to settle on.
"She's exceptionally good as an actress; one can see she's studied Kaulbach," said a diplomatic attaché in the group round the ambassador's wife. "Did you notice the way she fell?..."

"Oh, please, let's not talk about Nilsson! No one can possibly say anything new about her," said a fat, red-faced, flaxen-headed lady, without eyebrows and chignon, wearing an old silk dress. This was Princess Myakaya, noted for her simplicity and the roughness of her manners, and nicknamed _enfant terrible_. Princess Myakaya, seated in the middle between the two groups and listening to both, took part in the conversation first of one and then of the other. "Three people have used that exact phrase about Kaulbach to me today already, as though they had all made a pact about it. And I can't see why they liked that remark so much."
The conversation was cut short by this observation, and a new subject had to be thought of again.

"Do tell me something amusing but not spiteful," said the ambassador's wife, a great proficient in the art of that elegant conversation the English call _small talk_. She addressed the attaché, who was now at a loss for what to begin upon.

"They say that's a difficult task — that nothing's amusing that isn't spiteful," he began with a smile. "But I'll try. Give me a subject. It all lies in the subject. Once a subject's given me, it's easy to spin something round it. I often think the celebrated talkers of the last century would find it difficult to talk cleverly now. Everything clever is so stale..."
"That was said long ago," the ambassador's wife cut in, laughing.
The conversation began amiably, but precisely because it was too amiable, it came to a stop again. They had to fall back on the sure, never-failing topic — gossip.
"Don't you think there's something Louis Quinze about Tushkevitch?" he said, glancing toward a handsome, fair-haired young man standing at the table.
"Oh yes! He's in the same style as the drawing-room — and that's why he's so often here."
This conversation was kept up, because it rested on allusions to what could not be openly discussed in that room — that is, the relations between Tushkevitch and their hostess.

Round the samovar and the hostess, meanwhile, the conversation had been wavering in just the same way among the three inevitable topics: the latest piece of public news, the theater, and scandal. It too came finally to rest on the last topic — that is, ill-natured gossip.
"Have you heard the Maltishtcheva woman — the mother, not the daughter — has ordered a costume in _diable rose_ color?"
"Nonsense! No, that's too lovely!"
"I wonder how, with her sense — for she's not a fool, you know — she can't see how funny she is."
Everyone had something to say in censure or ridicule of the luckless Madame Maltishtcheva, and the conversation crackled merrily, like a burning faggot-stack.

Princess Betsy's husband, a good-natured fat man, an ardent collector of engravings, hearing that his wife had visitors, came into the drawing-room before going to his club. Stepping noiselessly over the thick rugs, he went up to Princess Myakaya.
"How did you like Nilsson?" he asked.

"Oh, how can you steal up on a person like that! How you startled me!" she replied. "Please don't talk to me about the opera; you know nothing about music. I'd better meet you on your own ground and talk about your majolica and engravings. Now, what treasure have you been buying lately at the old curiosity shops?"
"Would you like me to show you? But you don't understand such things."
"Oh, do show me! I've been learning about them at those — what are their names? — the bankers... they have some splendid engravings. They showed them to us."
"Why, have you been at the Schützburgs'?" the hostess asked from the samovar.

"Yes, _ma chère_. They asked my husband and me to dinner, and told us the sauce at that dinner cost a hundred pounds," Princess Myakaya said loudly, conscious that everyone was listening; "and very nasty sauce it was — some green mess. We had to invite them back, and I made them a sauce for eighteen pence, and everybody was very pleased with it. I can't run to hundred-pound sauces."
"She's unique!" said the lady of the house.
"Marvelous!" said someone.

The sensation produced by Princess Myakaya's speeches was always unique, and the secret of it lay in the fact that, though she did not always speak appropriately — as just now — she said simple things that had some sense in them. In the society in which she lived such plain statements produced the effect of the wittiest epigram. Princess Myakaya never could see why this was so, but she knew it was, and took advantage of it.

As everyone had been listening while Princess Myakaya spoke, and the conversation around the ambassador's wife had therefore dropped, Princess Betsy tried to bring the whole party together and turned to the ambassador's wife.
"Will you really not have any tea? You should come over here by us."
"No, we're very happy where we are," the ambassador's wife replied with a smile, and went on with the conversation that had begun.
It was a very agreeable conversation. They were criticizing the Karenins, husband and wife.
"Anna is quite changed since her stay in Moscow. There's something strange about her," said her friend.
"The great change is that she brought back with her the shadow of Alexey Vronsky," said the ambassador's wife.

"Well, what of it? There's a fable of Grimm's about a man without a shadow, a man who's lost his shadow. And that's his punishment for something. I could never understand how it was a punishment. But a woman must dislike being without a shadow."
"Yes, but women with a shadow usually come to a bad end," said Anna's friend.
"Bad luck to your tongue!" Princess Myakaya broke in. "Madame Karenina is a splendid woman. I don't like her husband, but I like her very much."
"Why don't you like her husband? He's such a remarkable man," said the ambassador's wife. "My husband says there are few statesmen like him in Europe."

"And my husband tells me just the same, but I don't believe it," Princess Myakaya said. "If our husbands didn't talk to us, we would see the facts as they are. Alexey Alexandrovitch, in my view, is simply a fool. I say it in a whisper... but doesn't it really make everything clear? Before, when I was told to consider him clever, I kept looking for his ability, and thought myself a fool for not seeing it; but the moment I said, _he's a fool,_ even if only in a whisper, everything was explained, wasn't it?"
"How spiteful you are today!"
"Not a bit. I had no other way out. One of the two had to be a fool. And, well, one can't say that of oneself."
"'No one is satisfied with his fortune, and everyone is satisfied with his wit.'" The attaché repeated the French saying.

"That's just it, exactly," Princess Myakaya turned to him. "But the point is that I won't abandon Anna to your mercies. She's so nice, so charming. How can she help it if they're all in love with her and follow her about like shadows?"
"Oh, I had no idea of blaming her for it," Anna's friend said in self-defense.
"If no one follows us about like a shadow, that's no proof we have any right to blame her."

And, having duly disposed of Anna's friend, Princess Myakaya got up and, together with the ambassador's wife, joined the group at the table, where the conversation was dealing with the king of Prussia.
"What wicked gossip were you talking over there?" Betsy asked.
"About the Karenins. The princess gave us a sketch of Alexey Alexandrovitch," said the ambassador's wife with a smile, as she sat down at the table.
"A pity we didn't hear it!" Princess Betsy said, glancing toward the door. "Ah, here you are at last!" she said, turning with a smile to Vronsky as he came in.

Vronsky was not merely acquainted with everyone he was meeting here; he saw them all every day, and so he came in with the quiet manner with which one enters a room full of people from whom one has only just parted.

"Where do I come from?" he said, in answer to a question from the ambassador's wife. "Well, there's no help for it, I must confess. From the _opera bouffe_. I do believe I've seen it a hundred times, and always with fresh enjoyment. It's exquisite. I know it's disgraceful, but I fall asleep at the opera, and I sit through the _opera bouffe_ to the last minute and enjoy it. This evening..."
He mentioned a French actress and was about to tell something about her; but the ambassador's wife, with playful horror, cut him short.
"Please don't tell us about that horror."
"All right, I won't — especially as everyone knows those horrors."
"And we'd all go see them if it were accepted as the correct thing, like the opera," Princess Myakaya chimed in.

title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Steps were heard at the door, and Princess Betsy, knowing it was Madame Karenina, glanced at Vronsky. He was looking toward the door, and his face wore a strange new expression. Joyfully, intently, and at the same time timidly, he gazed at the approaching figure, and slowly rose to his feet. Anna walked into the drawing-room. Holding herself extremely erect, as always, looking straight ahead, and moving with that swift, decisive, and light step that set her apart from all other society women, she crossed the short space to her hostess, shook hands with her, smiled, and with the same smile looked round at Vronsky. Vronsky bowed low and pushed up a chair for her.
She acknowledged this only with a slight nod, flushed a little, and frowned. But at once, while rapidly greeting her acquaintances and shaking the hands held out to her, she turned to Princess Betsy:
"I've been at Countess Lidia's, and meant to come here earlier, but I stayed on. Sir John was there. He's very interesting."
"Oh, that's this missionary?"
"Yes — he told us about life in India, the most interesting things."
The conversation, which her arrival had interrupted, flickered up again like the flame of a lamp being blown out.
"Sir John! Yes, Sir John; I've met him. He's a good speaker. The Vlassieva girl is quite in love with him."
"And is it true the younger Vlassieva girl's to marry Topov?"
"Yes, they say it's all but settled."
"I'm amazed at the parents! They say it's a marriage for love."
"For love? What antediluvian notions you have! Who talks of love in these days?" said the ambassador's wife.
"What can one do? It's a foolish old fashion that's still kept up," Vronsky said.
"So much the worse for those who keep up the fashion. The only happy marriages I know are marriages of prudence."
"Yes, but how often the happiness of these prudent marriages flies away like dust, simply because the very passion they refused to recognize turns up," Vronsky said.
"But by marriages of prudence we mean those in which both parties have already sown their wild oats. It's like scarlatina — you have to go through it and get it over with."
"Then they ought to find out how to vaccinate for love, like smallpox."
"In my young days I was in love with a deacon," said Princess Myakaya. "I don't know that it did me any good."
"No — I imagine, joking aside, that to know love, one has to make mistakes and then correct them," said Princess Betsy.
"Even after marriage?" the ambassador's wife asked playfully.
"'It's never too late to mend.'" The attaché repeated the English proverb.

"Just so," Betsy agreed; "one has to make mistakes and correct them. What do you think about it?" she turned to Anna, who, with a faintly visible resolute smile on her lips, was listening to the conversation in silence.
"I think," Anna said, toying with the glove she had taken off, "I think... so many men, so many minds; certainly so many hearts, so many kinds of love."
Vronsky was gazing at Anna, waiting with a sinking heart for what she would say. He sighed as though after a danger had been escaped when she uttered these words.
Anna suddenly turned to him.
"Oh, I had a letter from Moscow. They write me that Kitty Shtcherbatskaya is very ill."
"Really?" Vronsky said, frowning.
Anna looked sternly at him.
"Doesn't that interest you?"
"On the contrary, very much. What was it exactly they told you, if I may know?" he asked.
Anna got up and went over to Betsy.
"Give me a cup of tea," she said, standing at her table.
While Betsy was pouring the tea, Vronsky went up to Anna.
"What is it they're writing to you?" he repeated.

"I often think men have no understanding of what isn't honorable, though they're always talking about it," Anna said, without answering him. "I've been wanting to tell you this for a long while," she added, and moving a few steps away, sat down at a table in a corner covered with albums.
"I don't quite understand what you mean," he said, handing her the cup.
She glanced toward the sofa beside her, and he instantly sat down.
"Yes, I've been meaning to tell you," she said, not looking at him. "You behaved wrongly — very wrongly."
"Do you suppose I don't know I've acted wrongly? But who was the cause of my doing so?"
"Why are you saying that to me?" she asked, glancing severely at him.
"You know why," he answered boldly and joyfully, meeting her gaze and not lowering his eyes.
It was not he, but she, who was flustered.
"That just shows you have no heart," she said. But her eyes said that she knew he did have a heart, and that was the very reason she was afraid of him.
"What you spoke of just now was a mistake, and not love."

"Remember that I have forbidden you to utter that word, that hateful word," Anna said with a shudder. But at once she felt that by the very word "forbidden" she had betrayed that she acknowledged certain rights over him, and was, by that very fact, encouraging him to speak of love. "I've long meant to tell you this," she went on, looking firmly into his eyes, hot all over from the burning flush on her cheeks. "I came on purpose this evening, knowing I'd meet you. I have come to tell you that this must end. I have never blushed in front of anyone, and you force me to feel guilty of something."
He looked at her and was struck by a new spiritual beauty in her face.
"What do you want of me?" he asked simply and gravely.
"I want you to go to Moscow and ask Kitty's forgiveness," she said.
"You don't really want that?" he said.
He saw that she was saying what she forced herself to say, not what she wanted to say.
"If you love me, as you say," she whispered, "then act so that I may have peace."
His face lit up.

"Don't you know you are my whole life? But I know no peace, and I can't give it to you; all of myself — and love... yes. I can't think of you and myself apart. You and I are one to me. And I see no chance of peace ahead — either for me or for you. I see a chance of despair, of wretchedness... or a chance of bliss — what bliss!... Can it really be that there's no chance of it?" he murmured with his lips; but she heard.
She strained every effort of her mind to say what ought to be said. But instead she let her eyes rest on him, full of love, and made no answer.
"It's come!" he thought in ecstasy. "When I was beginning to despair, when it seemed there would be no end — it's come! She loves me. She admits it!"
"Then do this for me: never say such things to me again, and let's be friends," she said in words; but her eyes spoke quite differently.
"Friends we shall never be — you know that yourself. Whether we shall be the happiest or the most wretched of people — that's in your hands."
She would have said something, but he interrupted.

"I ask one thing only: I ask for the right to hope, to suffer as I do. But if even that cannot be, then order me to disappear, and I disappear. If my presence is hateful to you, you shall not see me."
"I don't want to drive you away."
"Only don't change anything — leave everything as it is," he said in a shaky voice. "Here's your husband."
At that very instant Alexey Alexandrovitch did in fact walk into the room with his calm, awkward gait.

Glancing at his wife and Vronsky, he went over to the lady of the house and, sitting down for a cup of tea, started talking in his deliberate, always audible voice, in his usual mocking tone, ridiculing someone.
"Your Rambouillet is in full conclave," he said, looking round at all the party — "the graces and the muses."

But Princess Betsy could not endure that tone of his — "sneering," as she called it, using the English word — and like a skillful hostess she at once drew him into a serious conversation on the subject of universal conscription. Alexey Alexandrovitch was immediately interested in the subject and began earnestly defending the new imperial decree against Princess Betsy, who had attacked it.
Vronsky and Anna still sat at the little table.
"This is getting indecorous," whispered one lady, with an expressive glance at Madame Karenina, Vronsky, and her husband.
"What did I tell you?" said Anna's friend.

But it was not only those ladies; almost everyone in the room, even Princess Myakaya and Betsy herself, glanced several times in the direction of the two who had withdrawn from the general circle, as though it were a disturbing fact. Alexey Alexandrovitch was the only one who did not once look in that direction, and was not diverted from the interesting discussion he had entered into.
Noticing the unpleasant impression being made on everyone, Princess Betsy slipped someone else into her seat to listen to Alexey Alexandrovitch, and went over to Anna.
"I'm always amazed at the clarity and precision of your husband's language," she said. "The most transcendent ideas seem to be within my grasp when he's speaking."
"Oh, yes!" said Anna, radiant with a smile of happiness, and not understanding a word of what Betsy had said. She crossed over to the big table and joined in the general conversation.

Alexey Alexandrovitch, after staying half an hour, went up to his wife and suggested they go home together. But she answered, not looking at him, that she was staying for supper. Alexey Alexandrovitch made his bows and withdrew.

The fat old Tatar, Madame Karenina's coachman, was having trouble holding one of her pair of grays, which was chilled and rearing at the entrance. A footman stood holding the carriage door open. The hall-porter held open the great door of the house. Anna Arkadyevna, with her quick little hand, was unfastening the lace of her sleeve, which had caught in the hook of her fur cloak, and with her head bent was listening to the words Vronsky was murmuring as he escorted her down.

"You've said nothing, of course, and I ask nothing," he was saying; "but you know that friendship is not what I want — that there's only one happiness in life for me, that word you dislike so... yes, love!"

"Love," she repeated slowly, in an inner voice, and suddenly, at the very instant she unhooked the lace, she added, "Why I don't like the word is that it means too much to me, far more than you can understand," and she glanced into his face. "_Au revoir!_"
She gave him her hand, and with her rapid, springy step she passed by the porter and vanished into the carriage.

The glance, the brush of her hand, set him on fire. He kissed the palm where she had touched him, and went home, happy with the sense that this evening had brought him closer to his goal than the last two months put together.

title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch had seen nothing striking or improper in the fact that his wife had been sitting with Vronsky at a separate table, in eager conversation with him about something. But he noticed that to the rest of the party it appeared striking and improper, and for that reason it seemed improper to him as well. He made up his mind that he must speak to his wife about it.

On reaching home, Alexey Alexandrovitch went to his study, as he usually did, sat down in his low chair, opened a book on the Papacy to the place where he had laid the paper-knife in it, and read until one o'clock, just as he usually did. But from time to time he rubbed his high forehead and shook his head, as though to drive away something. At his usual time he got up and got ready for bed. Anna Arkadyevna had not yet come in. With a book under his arm he went upstairs. But this evening, instead of his usual thoughts and meditations on official details, his thoughts were absorbed by his wife and something unpleasant connected with her. Contrary to his usual habit, he did not get into bed but fell to walking up and down the rooms with his hands clasped behind his back. He could not go to bed, feeling it was absolutely necessary for him first to think thoroughly through the situation that had just arisen.

When Alexey Alexandrovitch had decided he had to talk to his wife about it, it had seemed a very easy and simple thing. But now, as he began to think over the question that had just arisen, it appeared very complicated and difficult.

Alexey Alexandrovitch was not a jealous man. Jealousy according to his notions was an insult to one's wife, and one ought to have confidence in one's wife. Why one ought to have confidence — that is, complete conviction that his young wife would always love him — he did not ask himself. But he had no experience of a lack of confidence, because he had confidence in her, and told himself that he ought to. Now, although his conviction that jealousy was a shameful feeling and that one ought to feel confidence had not broken down, he felt that he was standing face to face with something illogical and irrational, and did not know what to do. Alexey Alexandrovitch was standing face to face with life — with the possibility of his wife loving someone other than himself — and this seemed to him very irrational and incomprehensible, because it was life itself. All his life Alexey Alexandrovitch had lived and worked in official spheres, having to do with the reflection of life. And every time he had stumbled against life itself he had shrunk from it. Now he felt something akin to what a man might feel who, while calmly crossing a chasm by a bridge, suddenly discovers that the bridge is broken, and that there is a chasm below. That chasm was life itself; the bridge was the artificial life in which Alexey Alexandrovitch had been living. For the first time the question of the possibility of his wife's loving someone else presented itself to him, and he was horrified at it.

He did not undress, but walked up and down with his regular tread over the resounding parquet of the dining-room — where one lamp was burning — over the carpet of the dark drawing-room, where the light was reflected on the big new portrait of himself hanging over the sofa, and across her boudoir, where two candles were burning, lighting up the portraits of her parents and women friends and the pretty knick-knacks on her writing-table that he knew so well. He walked across her boudoir to the bedroom door and turned back again. At each turn in his walk, especially on the parquet of the lit dining-room, he halted and said to himself, "Yes, I must decide this and put a stop to it; I must express my view of it and my decision." And he turned back again. "But express what — what decision?" he asked himself in the drawing-room, and could find no reply. "But after all," he asked himself before turning into the boudoir, "what has happened? Nothing. She talked a long while with him. But what of that? Surely women in society can talk to whom they please. And then, jealousy lowers both me and her," he told himself as he went into her boudoir; but this dictum, which had always carried such weight with him before, now had no weight and no meaning at all. And from the bedroom door he turned back again; but as he entered the dark drawing-room some inner voice told him that this was not so, and that if others had noticed it, that showed there was something. And he said to himself again in the dining-room, "Yes, I must decide and put a stop to it, and express my view of it..." And again at the turn in the drawing-room he asked himself, "Decide how?" And again he asked himself, "What has happened?" and answered, "Nothing," and reminded himself that jealousy was a feeling insulting to his wife; but again in the drawing-room he was convinced that something had happened. His thoughts, like his body, went round a complete circle without coming upon anything new. He noticed this, rubbed his forehead, and sat down in her boudoir.

There, looking at her table with the malachite blotting case lying on top and an unfinished letter, his thoughts suddenly shifted. He began to think of her, of what she was thinking and feeling. For the first time he pictured to himself vividly her personal life, her ideas, her wishes, and the idea that she could and should have a separate life of her own struck him as so alarming that he hurried to dispel it. It was the chasm he was afraid to peer into. To put himself, in thought and feeling, in another person's place was a spiritual exercise not natural to Alexey Alexandrovitch. He regarded this spiritual exercise as a harmful and dangerous abuse of the imagination.

"And the worst of it all," he thought, "is that just now, at the very moment when my great work is approaching completion" (he was thinking of the project he was putting forward at that time), "when I need all my mental peace and all my energy, just now this stupid worry has to fall on me. But what's to be done? I'm not one of those men who submit to uneasiness and worry without having the strength of character to face them."
"I must think it over, come to a decision, and put it out of my mind," he said aloud.

"The question of her feelings, of what has happened and may be happening in her soul, is not my affair; that's the affair of her conscience and falls under the head of religion," he said to himself, taking consolation in the sense that he had found the division of regulating principles under which this new circumstance properly belonged.

"And so," Alexey Alexandrovitch told himself, "questions about her feelings and so on are questions for her conscience, with which I can have nothing to do. My duty is clearly defined. As the head of the family, I am the person bound in duty to guide her, and so, in part, the person responsible; I am bound to point out the danger I see, to warn her — even to use my authority. I must speak plainly to her." And everything he would say tonight to his wife took clear shape in Alexey Alexandrovitch's head. Thinking over what he would say, he somewhat regretted that he should have to use his time and mental powers for domestic consumption, with so little to show for it; but in spite of that, the form and content of the speech before him shaped itself as clearly and distinctly in his head as a ministerial report.

"I must lay out fully the following points: first, the value to be attached to public opinion and to decorum; secondly, the religious significance of marriage; thirdly, if need be, the calamity that may follow for our son; fourthly, the unhappiness likely to result for herself." And, interlacing his fingers, Alexey Alexandrovitch stretched them, and the joints cracked. This trick, a bad habit — the cracking of his fingers — always soothed him, and gave precision to his thoughts, which he so badly needed now.
There was the sound of a carriage driving up to the front door. Alexey Alexandrovitch halted in the middle of the room.

A woman's step was heard climbing the stairs. Alexey Alexandrovitch, his speech at the ready, stood with his crossed fingers pressed together, waiting to see whether another crack would come. One joint cracked.
Already from the sound of light steps on the stairs he could tell she was close, and though pleased with his speech, he felt frightened of the explanation that lay ahead of him...

title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Anna came in with hanging head, playing with the tassels of her hood. Her face was brilliant and glowing; but this glow was not one of brightness — it suggested the fearful glow of a fire burning in the middle of a dark night. When she saw her husband, Anna raised her head and smiled, as though she had just woken up.

"You're not in bed? What a wonder!" she said, letting fall her hood, and without stopping she went on into the dressing-room. "It's late, Alexey Alexandrovitch," she said, when she had gone through the doorway.
"Anna, I need to have a talk with you."

"With me?" she said in surprise. She came out from behind the door of the dressing-room and looked at him. "Why — what is it? What about?" she asked, sitting down. "Well, let's talk, if it's so necessary. But it would be better to go to sleep."

Anna said whatever came to her lips, and was astonished, hearing herself, at her own capacity for lying. How simple and natural her words were, and how plausible that she was simply sleepy! She felt clad in an impenetrable armor of falsehood. She felt that some unseen force had come to her aid and was sustaining her.
"Anna, I must warn you," he began.
"Warn me?" she said. "Of what?"

She looked at him so simply, so brightly, that anyone who did not know her as her husband knew her could not have noticed anything unnatural — either in the sound or the sense of her words. But to him, knowing her, knowing that whenever he went to bed five minutes later than usual she noticed it and asked him why; knowing that every joy, every pleasure, every pain she felt she communicated to him at once — to him, to see now that she did not care to notice his state of mind, that she did not care to say a word about herself, meant a great deal. He saw that the innermost recesses of her soul, which until now had always lain open before him, were closed against him. More than that, he saw from her tone that she was not even perturbed at that, but as it were said straight out to him: "Yes, it's shut up, and so it must be, and will be from now on." Now he felt something a man might feel returning home and finding his own house locked up. "But perhaps the key may still be found," Alexey Alexandrovitch thought.

"I want to warn you," he said in a low voice, "that through thoughtlessness and lack of caution you may give people cause to talk about you in society. Your too animated conversation this evening with Count Vronsky" (he pronounced the name firmly and with deliberate emphasis) "attracted attention."
He talked and looked at her laughing eyes, which now frightened him with their impenetrable look, and as he spoke he felt all the uselessness and emptiness of his words.

"You're always like that," she answered, as though she had completely misunderstood him and had taken in only his last phrase. "One time you don't like my being dull, another time you don't like my being lively. I wasn't dull. Does that offend you?"
Alexey Alexandrovitch shivered, and bent his hands to make the joints crack.
"Oh, please, don't do that, I do so dislike it," she said.
"Anna, is this really you?" Alexey Alexandrovitch said, quietly mastering himself and restraining the motion of his fingers.
"But what is all this about?" she said, with such genuine and droll surprise. "What do you want of me?"

Alexey Alexandrovitch paused, and rubbed his forehead and his eyes. He saw that, instead of doing what he had intended — that is, warning his wife against a mistake in the eyes of the world — he had unconsciously become agitated over what was the business of her conscience, and was struggling against the barrier he fancied between them.

"Here's what I meant to say to you," he went on coldly and composedly, "and I beg you to listen. As you know, I consider jealousy a humiliating and degrading feeling, and I shall never let myself be governed by it; but there are certain rules of decorum that cannot be disregarded without consequence. This evening it was not I who noticed it, but, judging by the impression on the company, everyone noticed that your conduct and bearing were not altogether what one would wish."

"I positively don't understand," Anna said, shrugging. "He doesn't care," she thought. "But other people noticed, and that's what upsets him." — "You're not well, Alexey Alexandrovitch," she added, and got up, and would have gone toward the door; but he moved forward as though he would stop her.
His face was ugly and forbidding in a way Anna had never seen before. She stopped, and bending her head back and to one side, set to work taking out her hairpins with her quick hand.
"Well, I'm listening for what's to come," she said calmly and ironically; "and indeed I'll listen with interest, for I should like to understand what the matter is."
She spoke, and marveled at the confident, calm, natural tone in which she was speaking, and at her choice of words.

"To enter into all the details of your feelings I have no right, and besides I consider it useless and even harmful," Alexey Alexandrovitch began. "Ferreting in one's soul, one often ferrets out something that might have lain there unnoticed. Your feelings are an affair of your own conscience; but I am in duty bound to you, to myself, and to God to point out your duties to you. Our lives have been joined, not by man, but by God. That union can only be severed by a crime, and a crime of that nature brings its own punishment."
"I don't understand a word of it. And, oh dear, how sleepy I am — unluckily," she said, rapidly running her hand through her hair, feeling for the remaining hairpins.
"Anna, for God's sake don't speak like that!" he said gently. "Perhaps I'm mistaken, but believe me, what I say I say as much for myself as for you. I am your husband, and I love you."

For an instant her face fell, and the mocking gleam in her eyes died away; but the word _love_ threw her into revolt again. She thought: "Love? Can he love? If he had never heard there was such a thing as love, he would never have used the word. He doesn't even know what love is."
"Alexey Alexandrovitch, really I don't understand," she said. "Define what it is you find..."

"Pardon — let me say all I have to say. I love you. But I'm not speaking of myself; the most important people in this matter are our son and yourself. It may well be, I repeat, that my words will seem to you utterly unnecessary and out of place; it may be that they are called forth by my mistaken impression. In that case, I beg you to forgive me. But if you yourself are conscious of even the smallest grounds for them, then I beg you to think a little, and if your heart prompts you, to speak openly to me..."
Alexey Alexandrovitch was unconsciously saying something utterly unlike what he had prepared.
"I have nothing to say. And besides," she said hurriedly, with difficulty repressing a smile, "it's really time to be in bed."
Alexey Alexandrovitch sighed, and, without saying more, went into the bedroom.

When she came into the bedroom, he was already in bed. His lips were sternly compressed, and his eyes looked away from her. Anna got into her bed and lay waiting, expecting any minute that he would begin to speak to her again. She both feared his speaking and wished for it. But he was silent. She waited a long while without moving, and had forgotten about him. She thought of that other man; she pictured him, and felt how her heart was flooded with emotion and guilty delight at the thought of him. Suddenly she heard an even, tranquil snore. For the first instant Alexey Alexandrovitch seemed, as it were, appalled at his own snoring, and stopped; but after an interval of two breaths the snore sounded again, in a new, tranquil rhythm.
"It's late, it's late," she whispered with a smile. For a long while she lay there motionless, her eyes open; in the darkness she almost imagined she could see their brilliance.

title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: On the way home Levin asked all the details of Kitty's illness and the Shtcherbatskys' plans, and though he would have been ashamed to admit it, he was pleased at what he heard. He was pleased that there was still hope, and still more pleased that she should be suffering who had made him suffer so much. But when Stepan Arkadyevitch began to speak of the causes of Kitty's illness and mentioned Vronsky's name, Levin cut him short.
"I have no right whatsoever to know about family matters, and, to tell the truth, no interest in them either."
Stepan Arkadyevitch smiled almost imperceptibly, catching the instantaneous change he knew so well in Levin's face, which had become as gloomy as it had been bright a minute before.
"Have you quite settled it with Ryabinin about the forest?" Levin asked.
"Yes, it's settled. The price is magnificent: thirty-eight thousand. Eight straight away, and the rest in six years. I've been bothering about it forever. No one would offer more."
"Then you've as good as given away your forest for nothing," Levin said gloomily.
"How do you mean, for nothing?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch with a good-humored smile, knowing that nothing would be right in Levin's eyes now.
"Because the forest is worth at least a hundred and fifty roubles the acre," Levin answered.

"Oh, these farmers!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said playfully. "Your tone of contempt for us poor townsfolk!... But when it comes to business, we do it better than anyone. I assure you I've worked it all out," he said, "and the forest is fetching a very good price — so good that I'm afraid of this fellow's crying off, in fact. You know it's not 'timber,'" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, hoping by this distinction to convince Levin completely of the unfairness of his doubts. "And it won't run to more than twenty-five yards of fagots per acre, and he's giving me at the rate of seventy roubles the acre."

Levin smiled contemptuously. "I know," he thought, "that fashion — not only in him, but in all city people, who, after being twice in ten years in the country, pick up two or three phrases and use them in season and out of season, firmly convinced that they know all about it. '_Timber, run to so many yards the acre._' He uses those words without understanding them himself."

"I wouldn't try to teach you what you write about in your office," he said, "and if I needed to, I'd come to you to ask. But you're so positive you know all the lore of the forest. It's a hard thing. Have you counted the trees?"
"How count the trees?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, laughing, still trying to draw his friend out of his ill-temper. "Count the sands of the sea, number the stars. Some higher power might do it."

"Oh, well, the higher power of Ryabinin can. Not a single merchant ever buys a forest without counting the trees, unless they get it given them for nothing, the way you're doing now. I know your forest. I go there every year shooting, and your forest is worth a hundred and fifty roubles an acre paid down, while he's giving you sixty in installments. So you're in fact making him a present of thirty thousand."
"Come, don't let your imagination run away with you," said Stepan Arkadyevitch piteously. "Why was it none would offer more, then?"

"Why, because he has an understanding with the merchants; he's bought them off. I've had to do with all of them; I know them. They're not merchants, you know — they're speculators. He wouldn't look at a bargain that gave him ten or fifteen percent profit, but holds back to buy a rouble's worth for twenty kopecks."
"Well, enough of it! You're out of temper."
"Not the least," said Levin gloomily, as they drove up to the house.
